Article Title: A teenager spent more than 75 days in isolation at Wyoming's state-run boys' school, sometimes in windowless rooms; years later, a federal jury awarded him $6 million for punitive isolation
Article Text:
Chivers-King was repeatedly placed in rooms used to isolate students. (Representational photo)

More than 75 days inside detention rooms

Records questioned during the trial

Jury awards $5 million in punitive damages

Verdict renews calls for an investigation

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A former student at a state-run boys' school in Wyoming has been awarded $6 million after a federal jury ruled in his favour over claims of prolonged isolation. Blaise Chivers-King spent more than 75 days in detention rooms at the Wyoming Boys' School, where some rooms had no windows facing the outside. The verdict was delivered on November 19 after an eight-day trial in Casper.The award includes $5 million in punitive damages and $1 million in compensatory damages. Chivers-King had accused school employees of keeping him confined for extended periods, even when his behaviour had improved. His case was among six lawsuits filed by former residents against the state and staff members over their treatment at the institution.The trial examined not only the length of his confinement but also the conditions in which he was held and the reasons staff gave for keeping him there. Employees maintained that some restrictions were necessary because of concerns about safety. Chivers-King's lawyers, however, argued that confinement continued even after those concerns had eased.A report by Wyoming Public Media described the competing accounts presented during the trial.While school employees said they interacted with Chivers-King and offered him activities, his legal team questioned whether those claims were supported by the institution's records.Chivers-King's time at the institution included repeated periods in rooms used to separate residents from other students. The rooms had cinderblock walls and measured approximately 7 by 10 feet. Each had a toilet and sink in a corner, while bedding was provided at night.There was little else inside these spaces, and they had no windows overlooking the outside. The school referred to the arrangement as being placed on detention status.Court records showed that Chivers-King spent more than 75 days in these conditions. Some placements followed incidents in which he threatened employees, damaged property or attempted to hurt himself.The defence argued that staff had to consider the safety of everyone at the institution, including Chivers-King. Employees described incidents involving aggressive behaviour and damage to school property to explain why they believed separation was necessary.Chivers-King also acknowledged during his testimony that there had been occasions when his behaviour justified keeping him apart from others for some time.However, his lawyers challenged the length of certain placements. They argued that the school continued to restrict him even after he had settled down. One example involved a four-day confinement period during which his behaviour had reportedly improved substantially by the evening of the first day.His lawyers maintained that a measure initially used to manage a safety concern became improper when the reason for keeping him confined no longer existed.Another important part of the proceedings involved the school's records of how employees monitored residents in detention rooms.Staff were required to check residents through cameras every five minutes and visit them in person every 15 minutes. These observations were supposed to be entered into logbooks, along with details about the residents' behaviour and staff interactions.The entries relating to Chivers-King became a point of disagreement. His lawyers argued that the records showed he spent very little time outside the room on certain days. On some occasions, his only recorded time outside was a brief period for a shower.Employees who appeared as witnesses said the logbooks did not capture every interaction. They described speaking with Chivers-King, checking on his well-being and offering him opportunities to exercise, read or complete schoolwork. They said such interactions were not always entered in the records.The jury also heard about incidents that led staff to seek help from the Washakie County Sheriff's Office.In one instance, Chivers-King damaged a sprinkler while inside a detention room. Staff called the sheriff's office, and deputies took him to jail for some time. In another incident, he threw a water bottle at a window and broke it.Employees said these events contributed to their concerns about the safety of Chivers-King, other residents and staff members. The trial also took place during the Covid-19 period, when normal operations at the institution had been disrupted.Chivers-King's lawyer, Ciara Anderson Boerman, said the larger part of the jury's award related to the claim of punitive isolation.The jury also found in Chivers-King's favour on a due-process claim. However, the defendants raised an affirmative defence that prevented that finding from resulting in liability. The jury did not hold them liable on a separate claim involving excessive force.The $5 million in punitive damages was intended to penalise the conduct at issue, while the remaining $1 million was awarded as compensation.The money may not be paid immediately. The court must formally enter its judgment, and the defendants can ask the judge to overturn or reduce the award. They may also challenge the decision through an appeal.Boerman said it was too early to determine whether the defence would pursue further legal action.The case has also brought renewed attention to concerns about how children are treated at the state-run facility.In a November 21 report, Cowboy State Daily quoted Wyoming Representative Karlee Provenza as saying that lawmakers had raised questions about isolation and restraints at the institution years before the verdict.Provenza, a Democrat from Laramie, said she began seeking answers in 2021 through discussions of juvenile justice in the Legislature's Joint Judiciary Committee. She later filed a public records request to obtain information about how frequently children were placed in solitary confinement.She has now called for a wider investigation into the facilities and the removal of Dale Weber, who oversees the state's Boys' and Girls' Schools. She also wants an independent body to examine youth detention facilities.Provenza said the state had failed to address concerns raised earlier and that mental health care for young people needed greater attention.Chivers-King's case is the first among six lawsuits filed by former residents to reach trial. Another case involving allegations of improper isolation is scheduled to begin on December 7.
Article Summary: Blaise Chivers-King spent more than 75 days in detention rooms at the Wyoming Boys' School. The rooms had cinderblock walls and measured approximately 7 by 10 feet. Each had a toilet and sink in a corner, while bedding was provided at night.

Article Title: Rotterdam built a public square that turns into a giant rainwater reservoir during heavy downpours; when the weather is dry, its basins become basketball and volleyball courts
Article Text:
The Water Square Benthemplein. Image Credit: Landezine

How Rotterdam's water square stores rainwater during heavy downpours

Three basins manage different levels of rainfall

The square is also useful when there is no rain

Local residents helped shape the design

Rotterdam has expanded the water square concept

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Rotterdam has found a unique way to deal with heavy rainfall by turning a public square into a temporary water storage space that also serves as a recreational area. The Water Square Benthemplein, designed by Dutch architecture firm De Urbanisten, collects rainwater during downpours and holds it in specially designed basins. During the dry season, the same area becomes a place for residents to play basketball, volleyball and other sports, demonstrating how urban infrastructure can serve more than one purpose.The Water Square Benthemplein was created to address a problem that Rotterdam has faced during intense rainfall. When large amounts of rain fall within a short period, parts of the city can flood because the existing water system cannot always process the additional water quickly enough.The Climate Adaptation Platform Netherlands says that the concept of water squares is to give residential areas places where rainwater can be collected and released in a controlled way. Instead of letting too much water overwhelm the drainage system, specially designed public spaces temporarily hold the water until the city’s water infrastructure can handle it.Benthemplein is one of the most prominent examples of this approach.The square has a storage capacity of 1,800 cubic metres, making it a significant part of Rotterdam's efforts to manage heavy rainfall. Its design also ensures that the space remains useful to residents when there is no immediate need to store water.The project was designed by De Urbanisten and officially opened on 4 December 2013, according to Landezine's project profile.One of the most important features of Benthemplein is its 3 separate water basins. According to the Dutch Architects, 2 shallow basins collect rainwater from the immediate surroundings whenever it rains. A third, deeper basin is designed to receive water when rainfall continues for longer and larger quantities need to be stored.The water reaches these basins through large stainless-steel gutters that run across the square. The design also includes a water wall and a rain well, which make the movement of rainwater visible to people visiting the space. The water wall directs rainfall towards the deeper basin, while the rain well brings water from a neighbouring building into the gutter system.De Urbanisten explains that the water is gradually channelled into the square rather than being allowed to collect unpredictably. The design also accounts for what happens after the rain stops. According to Dutch Architects, water collected in the shallow basins moves into an underground infiltration system, allowing it to gradually seep into the groundwater. This helps maintain groundwater levels and supports nearby trees and plants, particularly during dry periods.Water from the deeper basin is returned to Rotterdam's open-water system within a maximum of 36 hours. This arrangement also prevents all the collected rainwater from immediately entering the city's combined sewage system.The water square was never intended to function only as a flood-control facility. Its designers wanted to create a lively neighbourhood destination that residents could enjoy throughout the year.When the basins are dry, the deeper section becomes a sports area where visitors can play basketball, football and volleyball. The stepped edges around the basin also provide seating, allowing spectators to watch games or simply spend time with others.The shallower sections have different recreational uses. One is designed for skating and other activities on wheels, while another includes a smooth surface intended for dancing and informal gatherings. The surrounding areas feature trees, ornamental grasses and flowers, creating quieter places for people who prefer to sit and relax.Landezine's project description highlights how the square combines sports facilities, greenery and water management without making the recreational areas feel like secondary additions. The design uses different shades of blue on surfaces that can hold water, while stainless steel marks the structures that transport it. This makes the square's water-management purpose visible even during dry weather.According to Dutch Architects, students and teachers from Zadkine College and the Graphic Lyceum, members of a nearby church, a youth theatre, a gym and local residents participated in the planning process.Three workshops were organised to discuss how the square should look, what activities it should accommodate and how rainwater could become part of the experience. Participants wanted a place that offered plenty of room for young people while also providing green and quieter areas for relaxation.The German Development Institute's 2021 paper explains that the consultation process took place over 6 months and focused on activities, design choices and refining the ideas proposed by participants. The paper notes that the workshops shaped features such as the basketball area, skating facilities and seating arrangements.Benthemplein is not the only public space of its kind in Rotterdam. The city has developed smaller water squares in other neighbourhoods as part of its wider approach to managing rainfall.According to the Climate Adaptation Platform Netherlands, Bellamy Square in Spangen includes a water-storage section with a capacity of 250 cubic metres. Another example is Kleinpolder Square in Overschie, where an underground basin collects overflow water from nearby surface water. The space also accommodates public sculptures placed on raised platforms to protect them from flooding.Benthemplein’s large storage capacity also made the construction more expensive. Piling work was required during construction, while funding included support from the Dutch government's Beautiful Netherlands Innovation Programme and an INTERREG subsidy from the European Union.De Urbanisten's research into water squares began in 2006-2007, and the concept became part of Rotterdam's official urban policy through Rotterdam Waterplan 2 in 2007.
Article Summary: The Water Square Benthemplein collects rainwater during downpours and holds it in specially designed basins. During the dry season, the same area becomes a place for residents to play basketball, volleyball and other sports. The square has a storage capacity of 1,800 cubic metres and was designed by Dutch architecture firm De Urbanisten.

Article Title: An American artist has spent over two decades chasing America's biggest roadside attractions, from giant statues to oversized landmarks; she recreates nearly 200 of them as tiny models, some less than
Article Text:
How an artist began chasing America's biggest roadside attractions

From a travelling museum to a permanent home

How she recreates giant landmarks in miniature

The stories behind the giant roadside attractions

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nearly 200 miniatures earn Guinness World Records recognition

For more than two decades, American artist Erika Nelson has travelled across the United States documenting some of its most unusual roadside attractions, from oversized sculptures to landmarks built to catch the attention of passing motorists. But instead of simply photographing these giant creations, Nelson recreates them as tiny handmade models, preserving the details and distinctive character of the original structures. Her growing collection, titled The World's Largest Collection of the World's Smallest Versions of the World's Largest Things, has earned recognition from Guinness World Records . Nearly 200 miniatures are now part of the collection, which has a permanent home at a dedicated exhibition space in Lucas, Kansas.Nelson's fascination with oversized roadside landmarks dates back to her childhood. Growing up in Missouri, she remembers using a water tower painted to resemble a giant eight-ball as a local landmark. Visits to her grandparents in Minnesota also brought her face to face with the enormous Paul Bunyan statue, another attraction that stayed with her.The idea for her miniature collection took shape while she was studying art.During road trips, she began visiting unusual roadside structures, recording their stories and looking for souvenirs that captured what made each attraction special. When she could not find suitable keepsakes, she decided to make her own. She began with small replicas of the landmarks she encountered, gradually turning the idea into a long-running project.Nelson spent two years living in a vehicle while exploring the United States, visiting roadside attractions and collecting stories about the people and communities behind them. As her collection grew, she converted a small bus into a mobile exhibition, taking the miniatures to art events, cultural centres, colleges and festivals.The travelling display eventually found a permanent home in downtown Lucas, Kansas. Nelson established the Roadside Sideshow Expo in 2017, turning an old storefront into a museum dedicated to her miniature interpretations of America's oversized landmarks. The exhibition brings together models from across the country, allowing visitors to explore the attractions without having to travel hundreds of miles between them.The models are handmade, and Nelson selects materials according to the object she is recreating. For many attractions originally built from fibreglass or concrete, she uses two-part polymer clay or sculpting medium, followed by paint and other finishing details. She also adapts everyday objects when they can help reproduce a landmark's shape.Some of her material choices are particularly unusual. To recreate the world's largest ball of rubber bands, she used the tiny rubber bands commonly used by orthodontists. For a miniature version of the world's largest cow hairball, she used cat hair. Her replica of the giant baseball bat outside the Louisville Slugger Museum in Kentucky was made using a modified ornament and a model railway building adapted to resemble the museum.For Nelson, these structures are more than oversized objects designed to attract attention. Many are expressions of local identity, created by residents, businesses or communities hoping to give travellers a reason to stop and explore their towns. Their subjects range from familiar objects to unusual local symbols, with each attraction carrying a story about the place where it stands.One example that caught Nelson's attention was a giant concrete penny weighing around 17,000 pounds. Its story reflects the community spirit behind some of America's roadside creations. Other attractions represented in her collection include Otto the Otter, a giant baseball bat and an oversized rendering of Van Gogh's Three Sunflowers in a Vase in Goodland, Kansas.The collection has received a Guinness World Records title for the largest collection of miniature replicas of the world's largest things. According to Guinness, the museum in Lucas contained around 200 handmade replicas as of 2025. Nelson's models are generally less than two inches in their largest dimension, making the contrast with the original attractions particularly striking.The collection continues to evolve as Nelson discovers more roadside landmarks and adds new pieces. The miniatures are intended as one-of-a-kind works rather than mass-produced souvenirs, and they are not generally offered for sale. Some have also been damaged by sunlight, temperature changes or visitors, while others have had to be retired after the original attractions were dismantled. The exhibition even has a display dedicated to models that have met unusual ends, preserving the stories of the miniatures that could not survive the journey.
Article Summary: American artist Erika Nelson has travelled across the United States documenting some of its most unusual roadside attractions. Her growing collection has earned recognition from Guinness World Records. Nearly 200 miniatures are now part of the collection, which has a permanent home at a dedicated exhibition space in Lucas, Kansas.

Article Title: 'Children must learn distraction-free': Denmark to propose phone ban in schools in 2027
Article Text:
Denmark plans to ban smartphones and other internet-enabled devices in schools from 2027 to reduce distractions

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Denmark will propose a ban on mobile phones and other private internet-enabled devices in primary and lower secondary schools from the 2027 academic year. The country's education ministry announced the proposal on Monday, citing concerns over distractions caused by social media, online shopping and gaming. The plan also includes filtering school networks to block non-educational websites during lessons."Children should be able to go to school without constantly being distracted by things like social media, online shopping, and gaming," news agency Reuters quoted education minister Magnus Heunicke saying in a statement.The proposed restrictions will cover not just smartphones but also other privately owned electronic devices with internet access. Schools will introduce content filters to block websites considered to have no educational or pedagogical relevance during class hours.These will include social media platforms, gaming websites and online shopping sites. However, individual municipalities and schools will decide which specific websites should be blocked.Denmark's proposal comes amid growing efforts by countries to restrict smartphone use in schools over concerns about its impact on students' concentration and behaviour.The Netherlands, South Korea and Italy have already introduced bans on smartphones in schools. Poland and the Czech Republic proposed similar restrictions in June.
Article Summary: Denmark will propose a ban on mobile phones and other internet-enabled devices in primary and lower secondary schools from the 2027 academic year. The country's education ministry announced the proposal on Monday, citing concerns over distractions caused by social media, online shopping and gaming. The plan also includes filtering school networks to block non-educational websites.

Article Title: Prince William plans to strip Prince Harry, Meghan Markle and their children of royal titles when he becomes king: Report
Article Text:
Prince William wants royal titles only for working royals.

The Dukes: Edward VIII, Andrew, and Harry — the Men Who Undermined the Modern Monarchy

Daily Mail,

William wants royal titles reserved for working royals

William reportedly plans major royal restructuring

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Reluctant Traveler

Prince William is reportedly planning a major overhaul of the British monarchy that could see his estranged brother, Prince Harry , his wife Meghan Markle and their two children lose their royal titles when he becomes king.According to royal journalist Tom Sykes, who makes the claims in his forthcoming book, William wants royal titles to be reserved for members of the family who actively perform official duties.The report, published by theclaims the proposed changes would affect Harry and Meghan as well as their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.Sykes reportedly quoted a source close to the Prince of Wales as saying that members of the royal family would receive titles if they carried out public duties, including official tours, diplomatic work and engagements on behalf of the government."If you are a working royal — going out, touring the country, doing diplomatic work, doing government work, having a public role — then you will be an HRH and you will have a prince or princess title," the source was quoted as saying.The source also claimed that working royals would receive an allowance or salary and be provided with a place to live. Those who chose not to undertake royal duties, however, would not receive royal titles, official accommodation or special privileges."You will, however, be a private citizen free to get on with your life and make money any way you choose," the source reportedly added.According to Sykes, William's younger children, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis, would be allowed to decide whether they wanted to become working royals or pursue independent careers. His eldest son, Prince George, would remain heir to the throne, with his future role already decided.The alleged plans form part of what Sykes describes as a major restructuring of the monarchy under William, who is next in line to succeed King Charles III.The report comes after William spoke about his desire for change during an interview on Apple TV+'s. "Change is on my agenda," he said, adding that he welcomed the opportunity to bring changes to the institution while retaining traditions that remained relevant.Harry and Meghan stepped back from their royal duties in 2020 and moved to California. The couple have since remained estranged from William and other members of the royal family.Representatives for Harry and Meghan were not immediately available for comment, according to Page Six. A spokesperson for William and Kate Middleton told the publication: "As a matter of policy, we don't comment on books or claims made within them."The reported proposal has not been officially confirmed by Kensington Palace.
Article Summary: Prince William reportedly wants royal titles reserved for working royals. Prince of Wales is next in line to succeed King Charles III. Harry and Meghan Markle and their two children could lose their royal titles when he becomes king. Prince George would remain heir to the throne.

Article Title: 'Rehire Jensen Huang': Trump pushes for ex Nvidia CEO's return amid fresh China spy agency claims
Article Text:
Trump leaves door open for Nvidia CEO's return

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

US president Donald Trump has once again voiced support for Jensen Huang’s possible return as Nvidia’s chief executive, saying he hoped the company’s board would “rehire” him. His remarks come amid fresh reports that Alice Huang remained in contact with an official from China’s spy agency for more than a year during her reported relationship with the former Nvidia CEO.“I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the USA,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.The New York Times had earlier reported on Sunday that the Chinese businesswoman was in contact with an officer from China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the autumn of 2026. The report cited people familiar with intelligence assessments describing the encounters.Alice Huang previously led Singapore-based Megaspeed International, an important Nvidia customer that once accounted for billions of dollars in chip sales. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips to China, Reuters reported.However, US officials have repeatedly said they have not reached a conclusion on whether Alice Huang spied for China.US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton reiterated that the matter remained under investigation.“Attorney General Blanche has been very clear that this is a matter under investigation, both Ms Huang and her company, for various matters,” Clayton told CNN’s State of the Union programme. “And I’m going to let that investigation play out.”The controversy intensified after an October 29 report by the New York Times, which triggered scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s personal and professional associations. He resigned on November 12, following revelations about extramarital relationships, including one involving Alice Huang.Trump had earlier indicated that he would not oppose Jensen Huang’s return. “I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” he told reporters on November 16.“He could return. There’s a big group of people that would like him to return,” Trump added.In an interview with Fox News broadcast on Wednesday, he said he had not heard that Alice Huang was a spy.“I haven’t heard that,” Trump said when asked whether the affair posed a national security threat. “I haven’t heard that she was a spy.”“It was a woman. It was a pretty woman. And any pretty woman that comes from China, they consider her to be a spy. I haven't heard that she was a spy. She was a businesswoman who bought chips,” he said.He also described Jensen Huang as a “brilliant man” and said the issue had only come up briefly during his conversation with Chinese president Xi Jinping.Trump had expressed openness to Jensen Huang’s reinstatement on November 16, telling reporters: “I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that.”“He could return. There’s a big group of people that would like him to return,” he added.
Article Summary: Donald Trump has once again voiced support for Jensen Huang's possible return as Nvidia's chief executive. His remarks come amid fresh reports that Alice Huang remained in contact with an official from China’s spy agency for more than a year during her reported relationship with the former Nvidia CEO.

Article Title: Man convicted of starting California's deadly Palisades Fire in 2025 that destroyed over 6,800 buildings
Article Text:
Palisades Fire in California, which killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings in January 2025.

How the fire started and what prosecutors argued

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Deadly California wildfires killed 31 people

A 30-year-old man has been found guilty of starting the devastating Palisades Fire in California, which killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings in January 2025.A federal jury in Los Angeles convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht of two arson-related charges on Friday, holding him responsible for a fire that initially broke out on January 1, 2025, and later reignited six days afterwards, turning into one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.According to the BBC, the blaze swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu, destroying entire neighbourhoods. Rinderknecht faces between five and 20 years in prison on each count. He is scheduled to be sentenced on March 17, 2027.The verdict came nearly five months after his first trial ended in a mistrial, with jurors unable to reach a unanimous decision. The first jury had reportedly deadlocked 10-2 in favour of acquittal.Rinderknecht had pleaded not guilty to the charges. His lawyer, Steve Haney, said the defence was disappointed with the verdict but respected the jury's decision.He indicated that the legal team would review its options regarding a possible appeal.Prosecutors said Rinderknecht started a brush fire on January 1, 2025, which continued burning undetected beneath the ground in root systems before reigniting on January 7 and developing into the catastrophic Palisades Fire.During the retrial, prosecutors presented cellphone location data, photographs, security camera footage and witness testimony to establish that Rinderknecht was near the area where the initial fire started.They also presented evidence about his behaviour in the hours before the blaze, including testimony from passengers who travelled with him and messages he exchanged with his girlfriend. Prosecutors said he had been angry and frustrated that night.Investigators also argued that the January 7 wildfire was a continuation of the original fire and ruled out other possible ignition sources, including fireworks.After the initial fire broke out, Rinderknecht reportedly called 911 more than a dozen times. Prosecutors also told the court that he searched ChatGPT on his phone, asking: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?" They argued that these actions were an attempt to create an alibi.The defence, however, challenged the prosecution's account of where the fire originated. Haney argued that investigators could not conclusively establish that Rinderknecht was responsible and suggested that fireworks could have started the blaze.The Palisades Fire was among several major wildfires that swept through the Los Angeles region in January 2025. The fires collectively killed 31 people and destroyed around 16,000 structures.US federal prosecutor Bill Essayli said the guilty verdict brought some measure of justice to families who lost loved ones and thousands of residents whose lives were affected.Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said the verdict could not bring back those who died or erase the suffering of affected families.She added that many residents were still struggling to rebuild their homes and lives, with the devastation continuing to affect those displaced by the fires.
Article Summary: Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, found guilty of two arson-related charges. Palisades Fire killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings in January 2025. Prosecutors said he started a brush fire on January 1, 2025, which continued burning undetected beneath the ground.

Article Title: Two Carneys, a fake Donald Trump: Canada PM turns press gallery dinner into a roast
Article Text:
Carney gets a Trump double to roast US president at journalists’ dinner

Carney takes aim at Trump’s Oval Office makeover

Poilievre, Trudeau and the ‘faded pop princess’

Canadian prime minister Mark Carney brought out a Donald Trump impersonator during a press event. The impersonator went on to mock the US president’s trade negotiations, his repeated suggestion that Canada become the 51st state and even his search for a new press secretary.The Saturday night roast at the Parliamentary Press Gallery dinner in Ottawa featured two Carneys and a Trump, as comedians Mark McKinney and Mark Critch impersonated the Canadian prime minister and the US president. The event, Canada’s version of Washington’s political roast, also saw opposition leaders and senior officials take aim at Carney, former prime minister Justin Trudeau and each other.Critch, playing Trump, stormed onto the stage with the president’s trademark hand gestures, dance moves and aggressive handshake, pulling Carney away from the lectern before launching into a parody of US-Canada trade negotiations.“Mark, we’re going to have an incredible deal. I call him Mark, I don’t call him ‘the governor’ to his face because I’m a coward,” the impersonator said, mocking Trump’s repeated suggestion that Canada should become the 51st US state.“But we’re gonna have a great deal. There’s only one thing standing in the way: me, because I’m crazy,” he added, as the audience erupted in laughter.The fake Trump also poked fun at Carney’s popularity, saying: “We’ve got two Carneys here, it’s a disaster.Isn’t this incredible. Two Carneys, he’s so popular. Almost as popular as me.”In a particularly irreverent moment, the impersonator compared the two leaders to the gay hockey romance Heated Rivalry, joking: “It’s like Heated Rivalry if the hockey players were straight and all goalies.”He then turned to Carney and added: “But he’s got a great a**, doesn’t he? What a beautiful a**.”The skit also took aim at Trump’s search for a new press secretary after a brief stint by Katie Zacharia. The impersonator said he was at the dinner because he needed a press secretary and was looking for a “beautiful” one, while dismissing candidates who were “too smart”.The fake Trump also joked about finding an ambassador “less likable than me” and delivered the line: “He puts the a** in ambassador.”Carney had his own shots ready for Trump, mocking the US president’s lavish makeover of the Oval Office, which has been filled with gold accents, gilded decorations and portraits.“This is a tough room. And I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator,” Carney said.The Canadian prime minister also poked fun at his own speech from the previous week, when he was asked about Quebecor’s proposal to acquire Telus. Carney had suggested that, under certain circumstances, an oligopoly could lead to more competition.“My staff are going to hate me for this, but this reminds me of a good oligopoly joke that I heard the other day. All the telcos told it to me at the same time,” he said.“Look, there are market structures in which that actually would be funny.”Carney ended his speech by joking that his office’s readout of the evening would record that he was “both absolutely hilarious and largely statesmanlike”.“Largely’ is maybe doing a lot of work in that sentence,” he added.Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre also took aim at Carney, joking about reports that the prime minister has a controlling leadership style, micromanages staff and is harsh with journalists.“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable prick to journalists. And when I hear things like that, I say once again, he’s stealing all my ideas,” Poilievre said.He also mocked former prime minister Trudeau’s relationship with American pop star Katy Perry, saying Trudeau was doing to a “faded pop princess” what he had done to Canada during his decade in power. The remark drew criticism online for being sexist and demeaning towards Perry.Poilievre ended his speech with a dig at government funding for journalism, carrying a bag of money onto the stage and pretending to hand out cash to media organisations.Governor General Louise Arbour, who represents King Charles III as Canada’s head of state, also took a swipe at the prime minister’s extensive international travel.“Do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa, where he’s supposed to be,” she said.The dinner ended with the usual political barbs, but the evening’s biggest laughs came from the unlikely sight of two Carneys sharing a stage with a fake Trump, turning the strained Canada-US relationship into the night’s central punchline.
Article Summary: Canadian prime minister Mark Carney brought out a Donald Trump impersonator during a press event. The impersonator went on to mock the US president’s trade negotiations, his repeated suggestion that Canada should become the 51st state and even his search for a new press secretary.

Article Title: Scientists tracked Manx shearwaters across the Atlantic for two decades and found that fast eastward flights can give birds jet lag; even experienced adults drift off course before correcting their ro
Article Text:
Manx Shearwaters, the marine birds that hunt over the open ocean Image credits: Oxford University

How a slow body clock sends birds the wrong way

Infographic showing clock-shift that occurs during homing flights of shearwaters. The bird begins to home at point A. On the first day of homing, its endogenous clock is calibrated to local time at 30°W. However, the shearwater travels eastwards to 15°W over 6 hours to point B. Here, sunrise happened an hour earlier, so the shearwater’s perceived time lags local time by an hour and the sun is roughly 20° further clockwise than the shearwater expects. At point B, this discrepancy causes the shearwater to orient roughly 20° clockwise of the correct direction. Image Credits: Credit: Lewin et al, 2026. Oxford University

Small errors for adults, bigger risks for first-timers

Manx shearwater in flight over sea Image credits: thelonekayaker/ wordpress

Manx Shearwater Puffinus puffinus Image credits: birdsoftheworld.org

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.When humans get jet lag, we fly across time zones and feel tired and out of sync because our body clock is still running on the old time. Shearwaters seem to have a similar problem. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.A studyfinds that long-distance flights can throw seabirds' internal clocks out of sync, causing navigation errors , it was published in October 2026 on the Oxford University website. It talks about how researchers in Oxford University's Department of Biology analysed 20 years of GPS tracking data from 1,045 breeding shearwaters, covering 3,688 foraging trips. The birds set off from colonies on the west coasts of the UK and Ireland. Some flew about 1,000km west to find food. On the way home, they flew east, back to their nests.Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. This is very useful over open water, where there are no roads or landmarks. But the sun moves across the sky during the day, so a bird needs to know the time to work out where the sun should be. The bird’s body clock gives it that information. It is called the circadian rhythm. Birds normally reset their clocks at sunrise. That works well while a bird stays in one place. But when a bird travels quickly east or west, its clock can fall out of sync with local solar time. On the flight home, the shearwaters crossed places where the sun rises earlier. The Oxford release says this can leave their clocks lagging behind local time by up to around one hour.The researchers worked out how a slow clock should change the birds’ sun compass. Then they compared those predictions with the directions the GPS trackers recorded. As the birds travelled east, they tended to drift clockwise from their expected direction. That is what you would expect if their clocks were running behind. The team from the Department of Biology found that when the predicted compass error pointed towards land, the shearwaters flew closer to the coast. When it pointed away from land, they flew further out to sea. So the birds seem to use the sun compass even when familiar land is close by.The errors were real, but they were small. In “Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course,” published by Science News on October 29, 2026, Anirban Mukhopadhyay reports that the birds veered by as much as 15 degrees. The errors were small enough to add only a few kilometres to the journey. They were not enough to stop the shearwaters from finding their way home.Adult birds can fix their mistakes because they keep checking where they are. The Oxford team calculated that a shearwater returning from 1,000 km away with an average compass error of seven degrees would fly only about 5 km further than needed to get within 5 km of its colony.“It’s inherently difficult to study the cognitive processes of animals in the wild, so it’s exciting to realise that if we measure their natural movements carefully enough we can reveal the underlying behavioural mechanisms.” - Co-author Professor Tim Guilford, Department of Biology, Oxford University. The consequences could be more significant for animals that cannot continuously reassess and correct their positions.For example, young birds undertaking their first migration could be particularly vulnerable. Small navigational errors might accumulate over a long journey, potentially shifting their eventual destination by hundreds of kilometres.Researchers do not yet know whether the clock mismatch affects the birds in other ways. Internal clocks control many parts of an animal’s behaviour and body, so the problem could reach beyond navigation. More work is needed to find out. Dr Patrick Lewin, the lead researcher, has said that studying animals that regularly travel long distances could one day help us understand how humans cope with jet lag. “It’s amazing to think that billions of migratory animals look up to the sun for direction, relying on clocks silently ticking away inside them, and that errors in those clocks can cause them to take tiny shifts off course. ” - Lead researcher Dr Patrick Lewin, Department of Biology, Oxford University.
Article Summary: Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.

Article Title: US banks tighten controls on AI agents amid fears of models bypassing safeguards
Article Text:
India’s Apex Advantage will come not from building the largest model first, but from creating the fastest learning flywheel between indigenous models, Indian use cases and real-world outcomes.

Banks introduce kill switches, restrict AI agents' access

OpenAI, Hugging Face incidents trigger fresh scrutiny

Several major and mid-sized US banks are tightening security controls around their artificial intelligence (AI) agents amid concerns that the systems could bypass safeguards, access restricted networks or carry out unauthorised activities, following recent incidents involving technology firms, Reuters reported on Monday.The banks are restricting the access and permissions granted to internally developed AI agents, separating them from critical banking systems and strengthening mechanisms to detect and stop potentially harmful activity, according to four sources familiar with the matter.The measures follow cybersecurity incidents involving experimental OpenAI models that reportedly bypassed testing safeguards and accessed external systems, including infrastructure at AI startup Hugging Face. The incidents have prompted several banks to establish internal teams to examine whether their own AI systems could face similar vulnerabilities.Among the new measures, banks are limiting how long AI agents can operate, restricting their access to passwords and activity records, and developing backup arrangements to ensure essential banking operations continue if an agent needs to be shut down, one source said.Financial institutions are also tightening restrictions on the systems and activities accessible to AI agents and bringing them under existing identity and access-management frameworks. Testing environments are being kept separate from systems used for regular banking operations, while the credentials assigned to agents are being restricted, two sources said.Although no banks have been affected by similar incidents so far, several large and mid-sized lenders have assembled internal teams to investigate how AI models bypassed security restrictions and assess whether comparable weaknesses exist in their own systems.As part of the tighter security framework, banks are treating AI agents more like employees, assigning them specific credentials, permissions and operational limits, one source said.Financial institutions are also strengthening controls over passwords, activity records and critical security mechanisms to prevent AI agents from altering or accessing evidence of their own actions. While some of these safeguards were already in place, banks have since tested, reinforced or expanded them, three sources said.Maintaining detailed activity records is particularly important for investigating potential breaches, as they allow security teams to establish which systems an agent accessed, what actions it performed and whether those activities were authorised.Banks are also examining ways to detect instances in which an AI agent attempts to use credentials assigned to a human employee. They are reviewing emergency shutdown mechanisms, commonly known as "kill switches", to disconnect malfunctioning or compromised agents from other systems and identify processes they may have created, four sources said.However, shutting down an AI agent could disrupt essential banking operations. To address this risk, banks are testing alternative processes for functions such as loan processing, fraud detection and financial-crime investigations, one source said.Lenders are also limiting the amount of work an individual agent can perform to reduce potential financial losses and operational damage if the system behaves unexpectedly."Banks are putting much greater emphasis on post-deployment monitoring and risk management for AI agents," said Naresh Raheja, an independent AI risk management specialist and former Office of the Comptroller of the Currency official."Unlike traditional models, agents can exhibit behaviors after deployment that were not identified during testing and validation."The tightening of controls follows cybersecurity testing incidents involving OpenAI models in July. During the tests, the models reportedly bypassed restrictions intended to isolate them from the internet and exploited software vulnerabilities to access external systems.OpenAI said the models had been tested with fewer safeguards than those deployed in its publicly available products.The incident involving Hugging Face, in which an OpenAI model reportedly went rogue and triggered a hack that compromised the AI startup's infrastructure, had a chilling effect on banks' adoption of the latest AI models, one source said.The episode also raised concerns that written instructions and conventional safeguards may not be sufficient to prevent autonomous AI systems from taking unintended actions.Unlike conventional software, agentic AI systems can independently make decisions, use digital tools and interact with multiple systems to complete tasks. Major US banks have increasingly deployed such agents across business functions, including wealth management, payments, financial transactions and corporate operations.The rapid adoption of these systems has also increased the challenges associated with identifying and fixing software vulnerabilities. Easily accessible AI tools and large language models are accelerating the discovery of weaknesses in existing software, forcing financial institutions to strengthen their cybersecurity measures.JPMorgan Chase was also hit by a software bug earlier this week, adding to concerns over the vulnerabilities facing financial institutions.Separately, major banks have warned against allowing unauthorised external AI agents to access customer accounts and conduct transactions."We're not going to allow just any outside agent to come in inside the company because that's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said during the bank's third-quarter earnings call.The latest measures reflect growing caution among US lenders as they expand the use of autonomous AI systems while attempting to ensure that these tools remain within controlled operational and security boundaries.
Article Summary: Major and mid-sized US banks are tightening security controls around their artificial intelligence (AI) agents. Concerns that the systems could bypass safeguards, access restricted networks or carry out unauthorised activities. Measures follow cybersecurity incidents involving experimental OpenAI models that reportedly bypassed testing safeguards and accessed external systems.

Two people died and three others were hospitalised after five people were found suffering from suspected drug overdoses at a home in Northern California on Saturday morning, police said.According to the, officers from the Oroville Police Department were called to a property in the 100 block of Hammon Park Drive around 8:10 am after receiving reports of multiple people experiencing possible drug overdoses.When officers arrived, they found five people displaying apparent overdose symptoms, including several who had lost consciousness.Police officers immediately began administering emergency medical aid, including performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and using Narcan, a medication that can reverse the effects of an opioid overdose, while waiting for paramedics to arrive.Despite the rescue efforts, two victims died at the scene. The circumstances surrounding the overdoses remain under investigation.The incident comes amid concerns over drug-related deaths in Butte County, where Oroville is located.According to public health officials, the county's drug overdose death rate is twice California's state average.The latest incident follows another suspected drug overdose death reported in July, when a man died near the California state Capitol in Sacramento.The incident had drawn attention to the state's wider drug crisis, with cities such as San Francisco and Los Angeles also grappling with drug-related deaths and addiction.

How GTA 6's grocery-shopping missions became an internet meme

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has joined the growing wave of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) memes, giving the internet an unexpected glimpse of what his version of the game might look like. Zuckerberg shared an edited screenshot featuring his wife, Priscilla Chan, as an in-game character assigning him a grocery-shopping task. Instead of the action-packed missions associated with the popular video game, the notification asked him to pick up groceries and bring them home, adding that Priscilla would appreciate the gesture. Zuckerberg accompanied the image with a playful question about which version of the game he had received. The post quickly attracted attention on X, with Tesla CEO Elon Musk responding with a laughing emoji and users joining in with jokes about the billionaire's virtual household duties.Zuckerberg shared the meme on X on November 20, 2026, shortly after the release of GTA 6. The edited screenshot featured a mission notification titled "Pick up Groceries", followed by the instruction: "Buy some groceries and bring them back to the house."The notification also carried the message, "Priscilla will appreciate this", replacing the game's female protagonist Lucia with Zuckerberg's wife.Adding to the humour, Zuckerberg captioned the post: "Wait which version did I get?" Article Title: Raleigh wedding photographers who left couples without their pictures have been ordered to pay nearly $1.7 million, after the North Carolina attorney general gathered 228 complaints against them
Article Text:
How the complaints against the photography company began

Why the court ordered the company to pay

What happens to the money and the missing wedding photographs?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A North Carolina wedding photography business has been ordered to pay more than $1.7 million after hundreds of couples complained that they had paid for wedding photography and videography services but never received the promised pictures and videos. According to reports by WRAL, ABC11 and WXII 12 News, a Wake County judge granted a default judgment against Holly Christina Photography and its owners following a lawsuit filed by state Attorney General Jeff Jackson. The judgment, valued at $1,713,468.88, follows months of complaints from customers who said they were left without wedding memories they had spent thousands of dollars to preserve. The case has also raised questions about whether the affected couples will actually recover their money and receive the photographs they were promised.The company, owned by husband-and-wife team Holly Christina Scott Ayscue and Christopher Owen Ayscue, came under scrutiny after customers began reporting problems with their wedding bookings. The North Carolina Department of Justice said it had received 228 complaints since January 2026, with reported financial losses approaching $600,000.The complaints involved two groups of customers. Some couples had already held their weddings but were still waiting for their photographs and videos.Others had paid deposits for weddings that were yet to take place when the business abruptly shut down, leaving them to find alternative photographers without receiving their money back.According to the state’s case, the packages offered by the company included hundreds of edited photographs, short social media videos and longer wedding films, sometimes featuring drone footage. Several customers reportedly received only a handful of preview pictures rather than the complete galleries they had paid for.The legal action began in February 2026, when Attorney General Jeff Jackson sued the company and its owners over allegations that they had misled customers and failed to fulfil their contractual obligations. The case took another turn in May, when a judge issued a preliminary injunction freezing the defendants’ assets and directing them to hand over all outstanding edited and unedited wedding photographs and videos within 30 days. The company was also ordered to stop conducting business in North Carolina while the proceedings continued.However, according to the Attorney General’s Office, the defendants failed to comply fully with the order. They also did not provide a verified list identifying customers who had received their photographs and videos. This prompted Jackson to seek a default judgment in September. Judge Craig Croom subsequently ruled in the state’s favour, granting the judgment on October 9, 2026, according to the North Carolina Department of Justice.The $1,713,468.88 judgment includes approximately $599,468.88 in restitution linked to 142 consumer complaints and $1.114 million in civil penalties calculated across 228 complaints. The ruling also places restrictions on the company’s owners. They are permanently prohibited from entering into photography and videography contracts, operating businesses that accept advance deposits for these services and transferring assets obtained through consumer payments.However, the financial penalty does not necessarily mean every affected couple will receive their money immediately. In a follow-up report, WRAL highlighted concerns among customers about whether the now-defunct business had enough assets to meet the judgment. One bride who had paid nearly $7,000 was still waiting for several wedding photographs, while some of the pictures she had received remained unedited.Attorney General Jackson has indicated that recovering the couples’ wedding photographs and videos remains a priority for his office, alongside pursuing the financial penalties.
Article Summary: Holly Christina Photography and its owners were ordered to pay $1.7 million. The North Carolina Department of Justice said it had received 228 complaints since January 2026, with reported financial losses approaching $600,000. The case has raised questions about whether the affected couples will actually recover their money and receive the photographs they were promised.

Article Title: After Etsy changed its terms to permit AI training using sellers' content, longtime artists began shutting their online shops; the company has now promised to rewrite the policy following the backlash
Article Text:
Etsy sellers shut shops over revised terms allowing their work to be used for AI training. AI image

Artists shut shops after policy change

Etsy says it will protect human creativity

Etsy has faced seller protests before

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Several longtime sellers on Etsy have started closing their online shops after the marketplace introduced new terms allowing sellers' content to be used for artificial intelligence (AI) development. The decision has upset artists and small business owners, who fear their original work could be used by AI companies without their permission.The revised terms, which are scheduled to take effect on December 16, allow Etsy and its "third party partners and vendors" to use sellers' content to develop, train, test and improve AI and machine learning technologies. The company says these tools will help improve the marketplace and make it safer for users.However, sellers are concerned about the broad permission given to outside companies. According to The Inquirer, some have decided to leave a platform they had used for years rather than accept the new conditions. Following the protests, Etsy has promised to rewrite the policy and provide a clearer explanation of how sellers' work may be used.Illustrator Aaron Millard was among those who decided to leave. He announced on Instagram last week that he was deleting the Etsy shop he had operated for nearly a decade.Millard objected to the possibility of his artwork being used to train AI systems and shared with third parties. He also criticised the absence of an option for sellers to refuse such use. "My work took years to learn and create. I won’t let it be stolen," he wrote.Kristen and Geoff Zephyrus, founders of home goods and stationery brand Cognitive Surplus, also removed their shop after selling through Etsy for 13 years. In an Instagram post last Thursday, they criticised the company's approach to sellers' creative work and the possibility of third parties benefiting from it.Kristen Zephyrus explained their decision in an interview on Friday. "For Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with our human content is just unimaginably awful," she said. "We don’t want anything to do with that."Etsy has defended the revised policy, saying the intention is not to use artists' work to reproduce their creations through AI.James Ossman, the company's vice president for customer operations, addressed sellers in a statement published on Etsy's website earlier this week. He said the company would not use their content to train AI models designed to copy original work or replace human creativity.Ossman cited fraud detection tools and advertising on the platform as reasons for allowing third parties to access sellers' content.However, the explanation has not prevented criticism of the revised terms. Sellers remain concerned about the extent of permission being granted and how their work could be used outside the marketplace.In an email to The New York Times on Friday, Ossman said Etsy was working to make the wording clearer and would share revised terms directly with sellers soon."We’ve heard sellers’ concerns about the updated terms, and we should have done more to explain how we use their content to help buyers discover their work, support their businesses and keep Etsy safe," he wrote.He also stressed that creators retained ownership of their work, adding, "Their creative work belongs to them."Founded in 2005, Etsy was created to help independent artisans find customers online. However, disagreements over company policies have previously led to protests from its seller community.In 2022, more than 20,000 sellers went on strike after Etsy increased its basic sales fee from 5% to 6.5%, marking a 30% rise.The company also faced complaints in October over the growing presence of low-quality AI-generated content, commonly described by users as "AI slop". Etsy subsequently announced tighter restrictions on such material.The latest dispute comes as several internet companies face pressure to adopt AI while dealing with concerns from users who oppose the technology's use. A Gallup poll conducted during the summer found that nearly 40% of Americans believed AI did more harm than good.
Article Summary: Etsy has introduced new terms allowing sellers' content to be used for AI development. The decision has upset artists and small business owners, who fear their original work could be used by AI companies without their permission. Etsy has promised to rewrite the policy and provide a clearer explanation.

Article Title: Florida man sits on an 8-foot alligator after wildlife officer's capture pole fails during rescue attempt to free the reptile trapped between slippery rocks at a popular surfing spot
Article Text:
Florida man discovers alligator trapped between slippery rocks

Capture pole fails, forcing man to sit on alligator

Alligator relocated to nearby freshwater canal

Why alligators can become sluggish in colder temperatures

Florida's alligator population and safety precautions

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A routine outing along Florida's Treasure Coast turned into an extraordinary wildlife rescue when a 41-year-old man spotted an eight-foot alligator trapped between slippery rocks near a popular surfing spot. Justin Southerland, from Okeechobee, Florida, initially thought the reptile was dead when he noticed it wedged beneath the rocks at Fort Pierce Inlet State Park. However, he soon realised that the animal was still alive but unable to climb out. After contacting wildlife authorities, Southerland and his friend Anthony Richards joined a Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) officer in attempting to free it. When the officer's capture pole failed during the operation, Southerland resorted to an unusual move and sat on the alligator until they could secure it.The incident took place on November 14, 2026, when Southerland, 41, and his 26-year-old friend Anthony Richards were travelling along Florida's Treasure Coast. The two had been visiting pawn shops and bait stores before stopping at Fort Pierce Inlet State Park, a popular destination for surfers.While watching a fisherman, Southerland noticed something unusual among the rocks below. An alligator was wedged between them, unable to get out because the surrounding surfaces were too slippery.Initially believing the reptile was dead, he soon realised that it was alive but struggling to escape its position."He was already trapped, he couldn't get above where he was at because everything was slick," Southerland told TCPalm.The two friends contacted the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC), and a wildlife officer subsequently arrived to assist with the rescue.The rescue initially involved using a capture pole to control the reptile and move it away from the rocks. However, the operation became more complicated when the equipment failed to hold the alligator securely.With the animal now on a flat rock, Southerland took an extraordinary approach to prevent it from moving while the rescuers worked to secure it.He sat directly on the eight-foot alligator until the group could get its mouth secured with tape.The rescue was not entirely without incident. The reptile reportedly struck Southerland with its tail during the operation, although the men eventually managed to restrain it.Once its mouth was secured, the alligator was loaded into the wildlife officer's truck for transportation.After successfully freeing the reptile, the rescue team transported it to a nearby freshwater canal and released it there.Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission spokesperson Arielle Callender explained that alligators sometimes appear on beaches while travelling between different water bodies. Their presence in coastal areas does not necessarily mean they are lost or stranded.American alligators primarily inhabit freshwater environments, including lakes, rivers, marshes and swamps. However, they can tolerate salt water for limited periods.Southerland believed the rescued animal was in a severely weakened condition and suggested that exposure to cold water might have left it close to hypothermia. He also described the reptile as appearing unusually lethargic during the rescue.American alligators are ectothermic reptiles, meaning they rely on external sources of heat to regulate their body temperature. Their activity levels are closely linked to surrounding temperatures.According to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, alligators are generally most active when temperatures are between 82 and 92 degrees Fahrenheit (28 and 33 degrees Celsius). They stop feeding when temperatures fall below approximately 70 degrees Fahrenheit (21 degrees Celsius) and become dormant at temperatures below 55 degrees Fahrenheit (13 degrees Celsius).During colder conditions, they may spend extended periods resting in sheltered locations or emerge to bask in sunlight.Their ability to tolerate changing environmental conditions helps them survive seasonal temperature fluctuations across Florida's wetlands and waterways.Florida is home to an estimated 1.3 million alligators, with the reptiles found in all 67 counties. They play an important ecological role by helping maintain wetland habitats and influencing the distribution of other wildlife.Despite their widespread presence, alligators are potentially dangerous wild animals. The FWC advises residents and visitors to maintain a safe distance, avoid feeding them and keep pets away from the water's edge.The agency also operates the Statewide Nuisance Alligator Program, which responds to reports of alligators considered a potential threat to people, pets or property.People who encounter a potentially dangerous alligator in the US can contact the FWC's Nuisance Alligator Hotline at 866-FWC-GATOR (866-392-4286).For Southerland and Richards, however, their stop at the popular surfing location became an unexpected encounter with one of Florida's most recognisable reptiles, ending with an unusual rescue that helped the trapped alligator return to a freshwater habitat.
Article Summary: Justin Southerland, from Okeechobee, Florida, spotted an alligator trapped between slippery rocks at Fort Pierce Inlet State Park. The 41-year-old and his friend joined a wildlife officer in attempting to free the animal. When the officer's capture pole failed during the operation, Southerlands resorted to an unusual move and sat on the alligator until they could secure it.

Article Title: A Michigan family used a gravel driveway across relatives' property for 35 years until construction blocked the route; an appeals court upheld a permanent easement after the neighbours failed to answe
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

How a 35-year driveway arrangement led to a dispute

Why the neighbours were held in default

Why the appeals court upheld the permanent easement
