A driveway used by a family for decades became the centre of a property dispute after neighbouring relatives blocked access during construction work. In Michigan, a family that had used a gravel driveway across relatives' land for 35 years took the matter to court after the route was obstructed. The Michigan Court of Appeals eventually upheld a permanent easement, ruling that the neighbours had not established grounds to overturn a default judgment after failing to formally respond to the lawsuit.In a November 19, 2026, unpublished opinion available on Justia, the Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court's decision in David Lee Shattuck v. Mark Shattuck. The appeals court found that the neighbours' participation in an earlier hearing about a preliminary injunction did not excuse their failure to answer the underlying complaint.The case involved adjoining properties owned by relatives. Mark and Michelle Shattuck owned one property, which also contained a gravel mine subject to federal regulations. David Lee Shattuck and his family owned the neighbouring parcel. According to the lawsuit, when the properties were purchased in 1987, the family began using a gravel driveway crossing Mark and Michelle's land to reach the main road. They continued using the route for approximately 35 years.Although the family had another driveway connecting its property to the road, David maintained that the alternative route was unsafe. The dispute escalated when construction work on the neighbouring property blocked the gravel driveway. David filed a lawsuit seeking recognition of property rights, including a prescriptive easement or an easement by necessity. He also requested a preliminary injunction to prevent further interference with access.At an initial hearing, Mark appeared without a lawyer, while Michelle did not attend. Mark disputed the claim that the family's alternative driveway was unsafe and argued that it remained usable. The trial court explained that the hearing concerned only the request for a preliminary injunction, not the underlying property claims. It denied the injunction because the available evidence was insufficient to make an informed decision. However, it directed Mark to maintain the existing situation and avoid further construction in the disputed area until the case was resolved.The court also discussed the outstanding deadline for the neighbours to file an answer to the complaint. Despite this, neither Mark nor Michelle formally responded to the lawsuit. At the plaintiff's request, the court clerk entered a default against them. David subsequently requested a default judgment. Although the neighbours appeared at the hearing and explained that they believed the case was over because the preliminary injunction had been denied, the trial court granted a permanent easement and required them to maintain it. David later died, and his son, Corey May Shattuck, was substituted as the plaintiff.After obtaining legal representation, Mark and Michelle asked the trial court to set aside the default judgment. They argued that Mark's participation in the earlier hearing showed that they had already defended the lawsuit. The trial court partially granted their motion because unresolved issues concerning damages remained, but refused to set aside the default on liability. The default judgment was therefore set aside, while the underlying default remained in place. Mark and Michelle then appealed.The Michigan Court of Appeals examined Michigan Court Rule 2.612(C)(1)(f), which allows relief from a judgment for another reason justifying it. The rule requires a party seeking relief to establish extraordinary circumstances and show that setting aside the judgment is necessary to achieve justice. The appeals court found that the neighbours had not met this requirement. It explained that Mark's appearance at the preliminary injunction hearing did not mean he had formally answered the underlying complaint. The judge had clearly distinguished the two proceedings and discussed the outstanding response deadline during the hearing.The court also rejected their argument that they reasonably believed the entire case had ended. The hearing transcript showed that the judge had instructed the plaintiff's lawyer to schedule further proceedings concerning the underlying lawsuit.Mark and Michelle additionally argued that the easement could expose them to obligations and potential fines under the federal Mine Safety and Health Act because their property contained a regulated gravel mine. However, the appeals court found that they had not adequately demonstrated why these potential consequences justified setting aside the judgment.Ultimately, the Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court's decision, leaving the permanent easement in place. The ruling addressed the neighbours' request to overturn the default judgment rather than independently determining the merits of the original easement claims.
Article Summary: Family used a gravel driveway across relatives' land for 35 years. David Lee Shattuck filed a lawsuit seeking recognition of property rights. He requested a preliminary injunction to prevent further interference with access. The trial court granted a permanent easement and required them to maintain it. The Michigan Court of Appeals upheld the decision.

Article Title: A Massachusetts father promised his son a 27-acre farmhouse, son paid over $200,000 towards it; years later, brother challenged his claim as five siblings fought over the inheritance
Article Text:
Representative image

A father's promise and a $70,000 farmhouse

Son paid more than $200,000 towards the property

Family inheritance plan reignited the dispute

Brother takes dispute to court over ownership

Massachusetts appeals court upholds son's ownership claim

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A decades-old promise over a sprawling family property in Massachusetts turned into a legal battle between two brothers after their parents died. Mark Iannuccillo had lived on a 27-acre property in Amesbury since 1978, when his father, Anthony Iannuccillo Sr. , allegedly assured him that the land would eventually belong to him, even though the ownership documents would remain in his parents' names. Mark contributed towards the down payment, paid his father more than $200,000 over the years and spent additional money improving the property. However, after his mother's death, the family trust provided for the property to be divided among five siblings. His brother, who became the successor trustee, sought to sell it, prompting Mark to challenge the proposed sale in court.The dispute centred on a 27-acre property at 94 Haverhill Road in Amesbury, Massachusetts, comprising a farmhouse, a barn and two garages. The property was purchased in 1978 for $70,000 after Mark expressed an interest in buying it, living there and operating a salvage-pool business.According to the court records, Mark found the property and approached his father about purchasing it. The two subsequently toured the land together and discussed the arrangement.His father, Anthony Sr., took charge of the purchase process and advised Mark on how to proceed.Mark contributed $7,000 towards the $10,000 down payment in April 1978. His father arranged the remaining $3,000 through Mark's older brother, Anthony, who had provided financial assistance to their parents over the years.However, when the purchase was completed on May 2, 1978, the property was registered in the names of Anthony Sr. and his wife, Loretta, as tenants by the entirety. Mark was not present at the closing because his father had told him that he did not need to attend.The arrangement was based on an understanding that the parents would hold the legal title while Mark would eventually receive ownership of the property. Mark believed his father would honour that agreement.Mark's financial contributions continued long after the purchase. From May 1978 until December 1987, he paid his father $600 every month in cash to cover the mortgage. Those payments amounted to $69,000 over 115 months, exceeding the actual monthly mortgage instalments.The financial arrangement continued even after his father refinanced the property in 1998 and obtained a new $75,000 loan. Between 1988 and 2001, Mark paid his father $10,000 annually, contributing another $130,000.In total, Mark paid approximately $200,000 to his father, excluding the additional money he spent on improvements and maintenance. His father primarily used the money from the refinancing for his own expenses, and Mark did not receive any of the loan proceeds.The property was also in considerable disrepair when the family purchased it. Mark moved there with his wife and children and undertook extensive renovation work. He restored the barn's foundation, installed new insulation, windows and floors in the farmhouse, refurbished its electrical and plumbing systems, renovated two bathrooms and installed a new furnace, radiators and lighting.Over the years, the property became known within the family as Mark's house. His parents, siblings and their families also visited it for social gatherings, used the garages for storage and jointly maintained a large garden.The situation changed after Anthony Sr. died intestate in April 2016. Under the ownership arrangement, Loretta became the sole owner of the property following her husband's death.She subsequently prepared an estate plan that included a will and a revocable trust. The original will provided Mark with a 50% share of the Amesbury property and allowed him to occupy it to the exclusion of his siblings for 365 days after her death. However, he would be responsible for the property's expenses during that period.In May 2017, Loretta signed a codicil reducing Mark's share from 50% to 44%. The trust created later that year reflected the revised arrangement.Loretta and Anthony Sr. had five children: Anthony, Mary, Mark, Elena and Christine. Under the trust's terms, the property was to be divided among them in varying proportions following Loretta's death.Loretta died in 2019, and the trust subsequently became irrevocable. Anthony, who became its successor trustee, began making arrangements to sell the property and distribute the proceeds according to the trust.Mark objected, maintaining that the property had already been promised to him under his father's 1978 agreement. He also pointed to his financial contributions and decades of work maintaining and improving the land.Anthony filed a complaint in the Massachusetts Probate and Family Court seeking a declaration settling ownership of the property and requiring Mark to cooperate with its sale.Mark filed a counterclaim, arguing that the property should be placed in a constructive trust for his benefit and that ownership should be transferred to him.The trial judge ruled in Mark's favour, finding that his father had agreed to give him the property and that the arrangement created a fiduciary relationship between them. The judge concluded that Anthony Sr. had breached that duty by accepting substantial payments and contributions from his son without eventually transferring ownership as promised.The court also found that allowing the property to remain part of Loretta's estate would unjustly enrich the estate at Mark's expense. It consequently imposed a constructive trust over the property for his benefit and ordered Anthony, as trustee, to execute a deed transferring ownership to Mark. He was also directed to reimburse the trust for the property's insurance costs.Anthony challenged the decision before the Massachusetts Appeals Court, arguing that the property had legally belonged to his parents as tenants by the entirety and subsequently passed to his mother. He also maintained that transferring it to Mark would undermine Loretta's stated inheritance plans.However, the appeals court rejected these arguments and upheld the lower court's decision on August 19, 2026.The court noted that the agreement between Mark and his father had been made before the property was registered in his parents' names. It also pointed out that Loretta knew about the arrangement and that the constructive trust had originated from the 1978 agreement.The judges further observed that Mark had contributed $7,000 towards the original down payment, made payments exceeding $200,000 over the years and financed numerous improvements to the property.The court concluded that the lower court had correctly recognised the constructive trust and that the property had not been properly transferred into Loretta's revocable trust because Mark's beneficial ownership already existed.The judgment was affirmed, allowing Mark to receive ownership of the 27-acre Amesbury property despite his brother's challenge to the claim.
Article Summary: Mark Iannuccillo had lived on a 27-acre property in Amesbury since 1978. His father had promised him that the land would eventually belong to him, even though the ownership documents would remain in his parents' names. Mark contributed towards the down payment, paid his father more than $200,000 over the years and spent additional money improving the property.

Article Title: US Army to detonate 5 tons of explosives in Iowa: The reason and the controversy
Article Text:
A sign marks the US Army Iowa Army Ammunition Plant as residents make plans for the US Army's detonation of a degraded stockpile of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa, US

Why does the Army want to detonate the chemicals?

Why is the detonation facing legal opposition?

Safety of the public Environmental protection Transparency with local residents Legal accountability 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

What are the potential health risks?

The US Army has rescheduled the controlled detonation of nearly five tons of unstable lead azide at a military ammunition plant in Iowa to Wednesday, citing weather conditions and safety measures. The decision comes as environmental groups challenge the operation in court and the Army seeks to invoke emergency provisions to proceed without an environmental permit.In a post on X on Sunday, the Army said the detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown had been moved to Wednesday “to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced”.“The Army and our interagency partners have been working around the clock to safeguard all Americans in the region,” the statement said. “The health and safety of all Americans has and always will be our first priority.”The operation was initially scheduled for Friday but has been postponed multiple times amid public concern and legal proceedings. The Army had earlier announced on Thursday that it would move the detonation to Monday, November 23.The material involved is lead azide, an explosive chemical used in the manufacture of munitions. Army personnel discovered several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide at the facility in March.According to officials, crystallisation had made the material unstable and increased the risk of an accidental explosion.The Army has argued that handling the barrels or attempting to neutralise their contents could trigger a fatal detonation. Officials have also warned that falling temperatures could further destabilise the material, with forecasts indicating temperatures below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1 degree Celsius).In a November 20 statement, Acting Secretary of the Army directed Army Materiel Command to postpone the operation until Monday, November 23, saying the delay would take the detonation to “the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop”. The Army subsequently moved it to Wednesday.The 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals had granted environmental groups' request to put on hold a permit issued by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) that cleared the way for the operation.However, government lawyers told the appeals court that the Army could invoke emergency provisions to act without a permit, arguing that “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.”Environmental groups, including the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, have challenged the Army's assessment of the risks and the alternatives considered.“The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency,” said Earthjustice attorney Thien Chau.An advisory warned that the blasts could release an air plume containing lead particles that may settle on the ground. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals,” it said.Residents have been advised to remain indoors, keep doors and windows closed, bring pets and livestock inside, and clean outdoor surfaces after the operation.The Army has said further details will be provided as the operation approaches.
Article Summary: The US Army has rescheduled the controlled detonation of nearly five tons of unstable lead azide at a military ammunition plant in Iowa to Wednesday. The decision comes as environmental groups challenge the operation in court and the Army seeks to invoke emergency provisions to proceed without an environmental permit.

Article Title: A Kentucky health-care fraud defendant owing $3.77 million in restitution tried to stop the $2.4 million sale of a company-owned building; a November 20 federal appeals court dismissed his challenges
Article Text:
Federal appeals court rejects a Kentucky man's bid to block the sale of a property (AI image)

How property came under court-appointed receiver

Why appeals court rejected his first challenge

Bankruptcy left Ehn without right to second appeal

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Court dismisses all three appeals

A Kentucky man's attempt to prevent the sale of a commercial property linked to his health-care fraud case has been rejected by a federal appeals court. Timothy Ehn, who owes more than $3.77 million in court-ordered restitution, wanted to stop a $2.4 million transaction involving a building owned by a company in which he previously held a 50% stake.The US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit dismissed three appeals filed by Ehn on Friday. According to the ruling , judges found that he had missed the deadline for challenging the sale approval. They also ruled that his subsequent bankruptcy filing had affected his legal right to contest decisions involving the company's assets.The property, located at 8780 US 42 in Florence, Kentucky, belongs to GT Enterprise LLC. It was the company's primary asset and had been put up for sale during efforts to recover money owed by Ehn and another defendant, William Siefert.The sale was approved by a federal district court on September 16 for $2.4 million. The transaction was scheduled to close on November 23. Ehn approached the appeals court seeking to prevent the deal from going ahead while his legal challenges remained unresolved.The dispute traces back to a health-care fraud case in which a jury found Ehn and Siefert guilty. Their sentences included financial restitution orders.Ehn was directed to pay $3,773,569.30, while Siefert was ordered to pay $1,968,763.10.The government subsequently sought to recover these amounts by placing liens on the defendants' ownership interests in GT Enterprise. Both men owned half of the company.The district court approved the government's request and appointed Michael B Baker to oversee GT Enterprise and its assets. The receiver was given responsibility for handling the company's property and was allowed to arrange its sale, provided the court approved the transaction.The receiver later approached the district court with a proposal to sell the Florence property for $2.4 million. The court accepted the proposal on September 16.Ehn objected to the steps taken during the receivership proceedings. Once the sale received court approval, he sought to prevent the money generated by the transaction from being distributed. He also wanted the transfer of ownership and other steps connected with the deal stopped.The district court refused to grant his request. Ehn then took the dispute to the Sixth Circuit, asking it to intervene before the scheduled closing.One of Ehn's challenges concerned the district court's decision to approve the sale. However, the appeals court found that he had waited too long to formally contest that order.The applicable deadline in a criminal case is 14 days from the date of the order being challenged. Since the property sale received approval on September 16, Ehn needed to file his appeal within that period. His formal notice of appeal was filed only on November 9.Ehn argued that a motion he had submitted on September 21 should count as an earlier notice of appeal. That application had sought replacement legal representation, more time and protection of the receivership's records and assets.The judges did not accept this argument. They found that the September application did not clearly identify the decision being challenged or specify the court where the appeal was intended to be heard. It therefore did not meet the requirements for a valid notice of appeal.Ehn also disputed the use of the 14-day deadline. He argued that since the government was recovering restitution through a civil process, the longer 60-day appeal period should apply.The court rejected this distinction. It said the underlying case remained criminal, making the 14-day deadline applicable. His November filing was consequently too late for the court to consider his challenge to the sale approval.The timing of Ehn's bankruptcy filing created a separate problem for his attempt to stop the transaction. He had filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy on September 16, the same day the district court approved the sale. In his bankruptcy proceedings, he listed his 50% ownership interest in GT Enterprise among his assets.The appeals court explained that this interest became part of his bankruptcy estate when he filed the petition. Under Chapter 7 proceedings, a trustee takes control of the debtor's non-exempt assets and handles matters concerning the estate.This meant Ehn could no longer independently pursue claims relating to his former ownership interest in GT Enterprise. The bankruptcy trustee was the person legally entitled to take action on matters affecting that interest.The trustee, however, had not appealed the district court's refusal to halt the property sale. Ehn could not file an appeal using the trustee's rights, the judges said.Ehn had also argued that the commercial property itself did not belong to his bankruptcy estate. The court said this did not resolve the issue because the relevant asset was his stake in GT Enterprise.That ownership interest had already become part of the bankruptcy estate. The court therefore found that Ehn could not demonstrate the legal standing required to challenge the order refusing to stop the sale.The Sixth Circuit concluded that it could not hear Ehn's challenges. His appeal against the sale approval was filed outside the permitted period, while his challenge to the refusal to halt the transaction failed because he no longer had the necessary legal standing.The court also dismissed a separate appeal concerning the district court's refusal to allow additional material and appoint legal counsel. It found that this decision was not among the types of orders that could be appealed at that stage.With all three appeals dismissed, Ehn's emergency request to suspend the property sale no longer had a pending appeal to support it. The judges therefore rejected that request as moot.
Article Summary: Timothy Ehn, who owes more than $3.77 million in court-ordered restitution, wanted to stop a $2.4 million transaction involving a building owned by a company in which he previously held a 50% stake. US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit dismissed three appeals filed by Ehn on Friday.

A brief eye movement by a New York lawmaker during a press conference with Mayor Zohran Mamdani has sparked bizarre conspiracy theories on social media, with some users claiming he could be a reptilian disguised as a human. The assemblyman has responded to the speculation, dismissing the claims and saying he has no explanation for the unusual-looking moment captured on video.Jordan J.G. Wright, a 32-year-old Democrat representing New York’s 70th Assembly District in Harlem, was standing behind Mamdani during a press conference at City Hall on November 20.As Mamdani addressed the media, a video appeared to show Wright smiling slightly before blinking and moving his eyes backwards in an unusual manner. Article Title: MacKenzie Scott gives $62 million to a marine conservation organisation working with fishing communities across the tropics; the funding will help protect 200,000 sq km of ocean and support a target o
Article Text:
How MacKenzie Scott’s $62 million donation will be used

What is Blue Ventures and where does it work?

Why small-scale fishing communities are central to marine conservation

What is the Frontline Community Fund?

Blue Ventures' 2030 conservation targets

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

MacKenzie Scott has donated $62 million to Blue Ventures, a marine conservation organisation working with small-scale fishing communities and local groups across tropical regions. Announced on December 10, 2025, the funding will support efforts to protect marine ecosystems, improve fisheries management and strengthen the livelihoods of people who depend on the ocean. It will contribute to the organisation's 2030 strategy, which aims to enable 10,000 fishing communities to lead marine conservation and fisheries management. The plan also seeks to bring 200,000 square kilometres of carbon-rich seas under effective local stewardship and improve food security and economic resilience for five million people. A significant proportion of the donation will support local organisations through the Frontline Community Fund.The funding will support Blue Ventures' long-term work with coastal communities, allowing local organisations to expand conservation initiatives and respond to environmental and economic challenges. These include warming seas, declining fish catches and growing uncertainty over fishing-related livelihoods.A significant proportion of the donation will be channelled to local partners through the Frontline Community Fund, which provides flexible, long-term financial support to organisations working directly with fishing communities. The funding model is intended to give these groups greater control over their priorities rather than restricting them to narrowly defined, short-term projects.Blue Ventures will work with local partners and Regional Advisory Councils to determine funding priorities. Its approach places particular emphasis on transparency, accountability and community leadership, with local knowledge playing an important role in decisions about marine resource management.Founded in 2003, Blue Ventures has spent more than two decades working alongside small-scale fishing communities and local organisations across the tropics. Its work focuses on helping communities manage fisheries sustainably, restore marine ecosystems and protect livelihoods dependent on coastal resources.The organisation began its work in Madagascar and has since developed programmes and partnerships across several tropical regions, including East Africa, West Africa, Southeast Asia and the Western Indian Ocean.Its conservation activities include supporting locally managed marine areas, restoring mangrove forests and seagrass habitats, improving fisheries monitoring and helping communities participate in decisions concerning their coastal waters.Rather than treating conservation as an activity separate from local livelihoods, Blue Ventures works with fishing communities to develop management approaches that protect marine resources while supporting the people who depend on them.More than 100 million people worldwide rely on small-scale fishing for their daily food and livelihoods, according to Blue Ventures. These communities depend heavily on healthy coastal ecosystems, including coral reefs, mangroves and seagrass meadows.Coral reefs provide habitats for fish and other marine species, while mangroves serve as important nursery grounds for marine life and help protect coastlines from storms and erosion. Seagrass meadows also support marine biodiversity and store carbon.However, these ecosystems face growing pressure from overfishing, habitat degradation and climate change. Rising ocean temperatures and declining fish populations can affect catches, reduce household incomes and threaten local food supplies.Blue Ventures' approach involves supporting communities in monitoring and managing their fisheries, restoring damaged habitats and developing locally led conservation measures. The organisation believes that giving fishing communities a greater role in managing marine resources can help protect ecosystems while maintaining the livelihoods they support.The Frontline Community Fund is a Blue Ventures initiative designed to direct financial support towards grassroots organisations working with coastal communities. It aims to address the difficulty smaller organisations often face in accessing long-term conservation funding.Through the fund, local organisations can receive flexible financial assistance, technical support and opportunities to share knowledge with other community groups. The initiative also supports the development of community-led data systems that help fishers monitor catches, understand changes in local ecosystems and make informed decisions about fisheries management.Regional Advisory Councils are another part of the model. These councils bring together representatives with local knowledge and experience to help guide funding priorities and identify organisations that could benefit from support.In 2025, Blue Ventures launched its first Regional Advisory Council for the Asia-Pacific region in Bali, Indonesia. The council brought together seven representatives from local organisations in Indonesia and the Philippines. The organisation intends to develop similar structures in other regions.The $62 million donation will contribute to a broader strategy aimed at expanding community-led marine conservation across tropical coastal regions by 2030.The organisation's targets include enabling 10,000 fishing communities to lead fisheries management and marine conservation, bringing 200,000 square kilometres of carbon-rich seas under effective local stewardship and improving food security and economic resilience for five million people.It also aims to equip hundreds of communities and grassroots organisations with the funding, skills, data and advocacy support needed to sustain their conservation work.The strategy focuses on building partnerships with local organisations so that conservation initiatives can expand while remaining rooted in the needs and knowledge of individual communities.The donation strengthens Blue Ventures' ability to support these efforts, with the organisation seeking to expand existing partnerships and help coastal communities take a leading role in protecting marine ecosystems and securing their livelihoods.
Article Summary: MacKenzie Scott has donated $62 million to Blue Ventures. The organisation works with small-scale fishing communities and local groups across tropical regions. It aims to protect marine ecosystems, improve fisheries management and strengthen the livelihoods of people who depend on the ocean. A significant proportion of the donation will be channelled to local partners through the Frontline Community Fund.

Article Title: Lahore tops global pollution ranking again as AQI crosses 500, eight Pakistan cities among worst
Article Text:
Choking under state neglect: Lahore once again ranks world’s most polluted city as AQI breaches 500

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Lahore once again ranked as the world's most polluted major city on Sunday morning, with its Air Quality Index (AQI) reaching 538, placing it in the hazardous category, according to Pakistani daily Dawn. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres, as severe smog continued to affect the province.Data from Swiss air quality monitoring platform IQAir showed Lahore at the top of the global major city ranking with an AQI of 538 between 9 am and 10 am. The reading exposed residents to severe health risks associated with hazardous air pollution.Karachi was further down the global ranking with an AQI of 180, followed by Cairo at 162.The pollution crisis extended beyond Lahore, with Kahna Nau in Lahore district recording the worst air quality in Pakistan at an AQI of 606. It was followed by Lahore at 538, Bahawalpur at 536, Sargodha at 392 and Gujranwala at 347, Dawn reported.Multan, Dera Ghazi Khan, Skardu, Faisalabad and Peshawar completed the list of the country's 10 most polluted cities.Lahore has repeatedly featured at the top of global pollution rankings in recent weeks.It recorded an AQI of 266 on Saturday evening, while the city had logged an hourly reading of 465 between 7 am and 8 am on Friday, as heavy smog affected several parts of Punjab.The continuing pollution has raised questions over the effectiveness of the Punjab administration's anti-smog measures. Lahore Traffic Police, however, has claimed that enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.Chief Traffic Officer Syed Abdul Rahim Shirazi said on Saturday that traffic personnel had issued challan tickets to 14,653 vehicles emitting smoke. Action was also taken against 10,306 vehicles transporting sand, soil and other materials without tarpaulin covers. Police penalised 31,618 unfit and dilapidated vehicles and took action against 272,760 overloaded vehicles, he added.Separately, enforcement squads from the Punjab Environment Protection and Climate Change Department conducted 84,370 inspections of brick kilns across the province between January 1 and November 18, Dawn reported earlier this week. During this period, authorities demolished 1,429 kilns, sealed 968 and registered 1,248 FIRs against violators.Between September 1 and November 18, which covers the peak smog period, the department carried out 29,999 inspections, demolished 519 kilns, sealed 494 and registered 408 FIRs. It also imposed fines worth PKR 101.45 million.The scale of Pakistan's air pollution is also reflected in long-term data. The 2025 World Air Quality Report put the country's average PM2.5 concentration at 67.3 micrograms per cubic metre, nearly 14 times the World Health Organisation's annual guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre, Dawn reported.The report also placed Pakistan among the world's most polluted countries, with an average AQI of 156.Globally, indoor and outdoor air pollution together account for an estimated 8.1 million deaths annually, making air pollution the second-leading risk factor for mortality worldwide. Outdoor particulate matter alone is responsible for an estimated 4.7 million deaths.
Article Summary: Lahore once again ranks world’s most polluted city as AQI breaches 500. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres. Lahore Traffic Police claims enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.

Article Title: 7 killed as tribal feud over forest ownership triggers gunfight in Pakistan

4 from one tribe, 3 from another killed in Pakistan forest ownership clash

Seven people were killed in a clash between two tribes over the ownership of a forest in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, news agency PTI reported, quoting police Saturday.The incident took place around 10pm local time on Thursday at Bilija forest in Battagram district, when armed members of the Gilal and Kaloch tribes confronted each other, leading to an exchange of gunfire.According to police, armed men from the Kaloch tribe took positions and opened fire, prompting retaliation from the Gilal side. Four members of the Gilal tribe and three from the Kaloch tribe were killed in the clash.The two tribes have been involved in a longstanding dispute over the ownership of Bilija forest, which has continued for several decades and claimed several lives in the past, police said.The Gilal tribe is associated with the Allai valley in Battagram district, while the Kaloch community belongs to neighbouring Kohistan district.Police said repeated efforts by the administrations of both districts to resolve the dispute and bring the communities together had failed to produce a permanent solution.The latest clash has once again raised concerns over the law and order situation in Imran Khan 's stronghold Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

United Nations high commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk has called for the immediate release of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan , raising concerns over his reported deteriorating health and detention conditions. Turk also urged the Pakistani government and opposition to de-escalate political tensions surrounding the case.In an interview with Christiane Amanpour on CNN, Turk said Khan's release could help build confidence between the government and the opposition.“I call for Imran Khan’s release. I call for his proper treatment, and I actually call for de-escalation. We need to diffuse the political tensions that are around this case, which means that a confidence-building measure between the opposition and the government could be his immediate release,” Turk said.His remarks come amid growing international concern over the health and treatment of the 74-year-old former prime minister, who remains in detention at Adiala Jail. They kill, abduct and torture at will.It is time the world acted, before they kill my father, the rightful, democratically elected leader of Pakistan,” Kasim wrote in a post on X.Amnesty International has also called for urgent intervention, citing restrictions on Khan's access to family members, healthcare and legal representation.The organisation said Khan had not been allowed to meet his family since December 2025, apart from two meetings with his sister in August 2026. It also said he had not been permitted to speak to his sons over the telephone since March 2026.Amnesty expressed concern over his reported solitary confinement and isolation from human contact, warning that the conditions could affect his physical and mental health. It also flagged reports of severe blood pressure complications and alleged that authorities had denied him access to independent doctors despite an August Supreme Court order directing that he be taken to a private hospital.The organisation also raised concerns over the health of Khan's wife, Bushra Bibi, alleging that she had been denied adequate treatment for an eye condition that could lead to vision loss.Amnesty said the treatment of the detained couple violated Article 10 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which requires authorities to treat people deprived of their liberty with humanity and respect.The organisation also called for the release of Khan's sister Aleema Khan, who remains detained at Kot Lakhpat Prison in Lahore. It said three of his sisters were detained on September 20 and 21 in connection with a planned Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf march to Islamabad.Khan had also issued an open letter to Pakistan's top judges on November 16, seeking urgent medical treatment and implementation of court orders. He alleged that he had been held in “torturous solitary confinement for up to twenty-two hours a day” since December 20, 2025.

Article Title: 'Bloodshed in Karachi, Hyderabad': Why Bilawal Bhutto is opposing plan to redraw Pakistan's map

Why is Pakistan considering more provinces

Pakistan Peoples Party chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari has strongly opposed the proposal to divide Pakistan into multiple provinces, warning against any attempt to split Sindh by force.He cautioned that such a move could trigger violence and bloodshed in Karachi and Hyderabad, Pakistan-based Geo TV reported.The proposal to redraw Pakistan's political map has reportedly found support among several leaders in the country's power corridors, including army chief Asim Munir and defence minister Khawaja Asif Speaking at an event at the Karachi Press Club, Bilawal said any forced division of the province would create social divisions and push ordinary people towards violence, Geo TV reported.“If the province is divided by force, society will be divided, it will lead to enmity, ordinary people will take up arms, and the bloodshed will not be limited to a single death,” he said.The remarks come amid discussions in Pakistan about reorganising its administrative structure by dividing its four provinces into smaller units. Article Title: $135 billion in debt, still getting loans: Who is keeping Pakistan afloat, and why
Article Text:
Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and chief of defence forces Asim Munir (Reuters file photo)

What World Bank’s International Debt Report says about Pakistan

Pakistan’s economic challenges

China: Pakistan’s ‘all-weather’ friend

Why financial institutions continue lending to Pakistan

Can Pakistan actually repay its debt

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What happens if creditors stop lending to Pakistan

The World Bank ’s International Debt Report 2026 paints a stark picture of Pakistan’s growing external debt burden, showing that, as of 2025, Islamabad’s external debt had nearly doubled from its 2015 level.According to the report, Pakistan’s external debt stood at $135.1 billion last year, up from $68.7 billion in 2015, marking a 97% increase in just 10 years.Pakistan's mounting external debt presents a curious contradiction. Its economy continues to struggle, and its dependence on foreign financing remains substantial. Yet, despite these vulnerabilities, money continues to flow into the country from some of the world's most influential governments and financial institutions.The question, therefore, is not simply why Islamabad keeps borrowing, but why its creditors continue lending to a country whose ability to generate sufficient foreign exchange and meet its repayment obligations remains a source of concern.The $135.1 billion, which Pakistan owed as external debt, was up 4% from $129.9 billion in 2024. Of the 2025 debt, around $107.1 billion was public and publicly guaranteed debt, while the remainder included private-sector and short-term external obligations.Of Pakistan’s public and publicly guaranteed debt, nearly $57 billion is owed to multilateral creditors, while bilateral creditors account for over $42 billion, with the remainder owed to private creditors.Among individual creditors, China is Pakistan’s largest bilateral lender, accounting for $22.4 billion in debt. It is followed by the World Bank, with $19.2 billion, and the Asian Development Bank, with $16.83 billion, among other creditors.The report also highlighted the burden of debt repayments on Pakistan’s economy. In 2025, Islamabad spent an amount equivalent to 33% of its export earnings on servicing external debt, while total external debt stood at 34% of Gross National Income.The report, therefore, highlights the challenge facing Islamabad: managing its growing external debt while ensuring that its economy generates enough foreign exchange to meet repayment obligations.Continued lending does not necessarily mean Pakistan’s economy is healthy. Nor does its growing debt burden mean the country is on the verge of default.The latest economic indicators present a mixed picture.The World Bank estimates that Pakistan’s economy grew by 3.7% in FY26, up from 3.2% in the previous financial year. The fiscal deficit narrowed to 2.6% of GDP, while the current account recorded a small deficit of 0.1% of GDP. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) also reported that Pakistan’s gross foreign exchange reserves had risen to approximately $21.5 billion by the end of September 2025.These gains, however, are offset by continued economic challenges. Economic growth has not generated enough jobs for Pakistan’s growing workforce. About 3.5 million people enter the workforce every year, yet unemployment stood at 7% in 2024. While nearly 18 million new jobs have been created since 2018, most have been informal, low-paid or self-employment opportunities.Poverty, too, has increased, with the rate rising from 22% in 2018-19 to 29% in 2024-25. An estimated 70 million Pakistanis are now living in poverty.The future outlook also remains challenging. The World Bank projected Pakistan’s economy to grow by 3.8% in FY27, a marginal increase from the estimated 3.7% growth in FY26. Headline inflation was expected to rise to 8.2% in FY27 before easing to around 7%.The data therefore highlights the economic pressures Pakistan faces and is expected to confront in the coming years.China being Pakistan’s largest individual creditor is perhaps unsurprising. Beijing and Islamabad are, after all, each other’s “all-weather friends.”China’s investment in Pakistan has largely been channelled through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), the flagship project of Beijing’s ambitious Belt and Road Initiative. Under CPEC, Chinese investment in Pakistan is estimated at $62 billion over a period of 15 years.Another important feature of this economic relationship is loan rollover, under which a creditor extends the repayment period of existing loans instead of demanding immediate repayment. China has continued to roll over existing loans to Pakistan, providing Islamabad temporary relief from its foreign currency obligations without reducing its overall debt.With Pakistan struggling to repay its Chinese loans, what explains Beijing's willingness to not only continue providing financial support to Islamabad but also roll over existing loans?Sushant Sareen, senior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation and an expert on Pakistan, attributed Beijing's continued support to the “strategic relationship” between the two countries.“It’s not just about an economic relationship between them. I think one of the reasons why the Chinese keep bailing Pakistan out and give them money is because of the strategic relationship that exists between them,” Sareen told The Times of India.Even CPEC, he added, was China’s plan to “prop up” Pakistan’s economy and make it more efficient and productive.Ultimately, the question is whether Pakistan can generate enough foreign exchange to service its growing debt, even with continued support from China.That Beijing is Islamabad’s largest creditor comes as little surprise. However, multilateral institutions such as the IMF and the World Bank also continue to play an important role in financing Pakistan.Since joining the IMF in 1950, Pakistan has received around two dozen bailout packages. Most recently, in October, the IMF agreed to release another $1.21 billion under its ongoing loan and sustainability programmes, subject to Executive Board approval.In a recent YouTube interview, former IMF chief economist Gita Gopinath was asked why the lender continues to bail out Pakistan despite concerns over its ability to repay its loans.Gopinath explained that the IMF’s role is to help countries facing economic crises and that it cannot simply walk away from them.She also emphasised that the IMF's decisions are taken by its member countries, including India. The decision to extend a loan, therefore, rests with the membership rather than the IMF's management.Sareen echoed this view.“Pakistan is a member of the IMF. It is the IMF’s job to bail out countries which are facing balance of payments problems,” he said.He, however, pointed out that political considerations could also influence the IMF's lending decisions.“India holds slightly over 2% vote share and that's not big enough to veto the loan. The Americans with 16% or 17% stake can actually do that, because with 15% you can veto any IMF loan. And clearly the Americans don't want to turn the screws on the Pakistanis. So, yes, to some extent it is a political decision to give money to Pakistan,” he argued.Sareen noted, however, that overall, the IMF largely operates within its economic mandate.Taken together, Islamabad's repeated reliance on the IMF underlines the extent to which its economy depends on external financial support.Pakistan's total external debt of around $135 billion does not mean the entire amount is due for repayment immediately. The debt has accumulated over several years, with repayments spread across different periods.The extent of Pakistan's reliance on fresh borrowing is evident from the figures. In FY26, it received $16.16 billion in external loans, while repaying around $14.44 billion in external public debt, including $11.20 billion in principal and $3.24 billion in interest, according to the ministry of economic affairs.The key question, therefore, is whether Islamabad can generate enough foreign exchange to meet these repayment obligations while managing its other economic needs.Sareen argued that the bigger challenge for Pakistan was not repaying its entire debt, but servicing it — having enough foreign exchange to meet repayment and interest obligations as they fall due.“Pakistans' problem is that they're not earning the kind of foreign exchange they require to service that debt. And the debt which they're taking on is increasing virtually every year. But for now, they're managing to tide it over. They managed to avoid default, but at a very high price,” he said.The challenge for Islamabad, therefore, is not just to keep securing loans, but to build an economy capable of meeting its repayment obligations without repeatedly relying on external support.Pakistan is often described as a country facing economic collapse and the risk of disintegration. Its continued dependence on external financing raises an important question: what would happen if lenders stopped extending fresh loans to Islamabad?The withdrawal of support from its lenders would not automatically push Pakistan into default or close to disintegration. Rather, it would face severe economic difficulties.Sareen warned that a default could trigger severe economic hardship, with Pakistan potentially spending three to four years trying to stabilise its economy and regain access to the international financial system. During this period, it could struggle to maintain imports and deal with foreign exchange shortages.But Pakistan continues to stay afloat — with support from international institutions, as well as countries whose financial assistance is shaped by strategic interests. Lending decisions also have a political dimension, with the interests and influence of powerful member countries playing a role.For now, creditors continue to extend financial support, even as concerns over Islamabad's ability to repay its debt persist.
Article Summary: Pakistan's external debt stood at $135.1 billion last year, up from $68.7 billion in 2015. China is Pakistan’s largest bilateral lender, accounting for $22.4 billion in debt. Pakistan spent an amount equivalent to 33% of its export earnings on servicing external debt.

The sons of imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan have accused authorities of subjecting their father to prolonged physical and mental torture in Adiala Jail, warning that he could die in custody without urgent medical intervention.In an interview with Sky News's Mark Austin, Sulaiman Isa Khan and Kasim Khan expressed concern over the deteriorating health of the 74-year-old Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder, alleging that he was being kept in solitary confinement for 22 to 23 hours a day, with little human contact and no access to independent medical care."We can see the path that this is taking. It's inevitable that eventually he will die in this cell. He will be killed in this cell if he remains there any longer without proper treatment," the brothers said.They also alleged that prison authorities had instructed guards not to speak to their father, adding that the isolation was being used to exert psychological pressure on him."I mean, we've been saying this for months. They're torturing him in the cell. It's physical and mental torture. It's at a point where they've instructed the guards not to even speak to him while he's in the cell just to, you know, maintain pressure and mental pressure on him," they added.The brothers said authorities had failed to implement an August 18 Supreme Court order directing that Khan be shifted to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for medical examination and treatment. The order had also called for increased family access, including regular telephone conversations with his sons."Nothing's changed at all, despite an order from the Supreme Court back in August for him to be taken and treated at a private hospital called Shifa International, and for increased family access to his family, calls with us, regular calls with us. But none of that has been implemented. And his health has just continued to deteriorate," they said."His blood pressure is now dangerously high, at about 193, I think. So he needs to be treated at a private hospital immediately," they added.The interview comes as Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges through an open letter, seeking urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi. He said his blood pressure had risen sharply and doctors had warned of the risk of a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest.In the letter, released by his party and lawyer Salman Safdar, Khan also alleged that authorities had failed to implement the earlier hospital transfer order. "I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he said.However, Pakistan's cabinet minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed Khan's claims, saying he had received regular medical attention and had been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad eight times for examinations. The government has also rejected allegations of solitary confinement and denied that Khan was being denied access to his family.

In a major organisational shift, Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has elevated its senior commander Rehman Gul to the post of commander-in-chief. Sources said his elevation carried symbolic weight given his past as a former captain in Pakistan army’s 19 Frontier Force (FF) Regiment.In 2010, Gul deserted the army, citing atrocities against civilians, and joined Aslam Baloch’s BLA, leaving the military brass flummoxed. Prior to assuming the top role, Gul served on the command council and led the Majeed Brigade, BLA’s operational wing which specialises in suicide bombings.Having graduated as a battalion senior major, Gul previously held military postings in Kotli in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir as well as North and South Waziristan, where he took part in military operations.The announcement also dispels earlier reports from the Pakistani military, which had declared Gul dead last year, a claim BLA didn’t validate. Adding a sensitive dynamic to the situation, sources indicate that Gul’s younger brother currently serves as a Major in the Pakistan army’s Signals Corps. Observers suggest that having a former military officer at the helm amplifies narratives of internal disillusionment among security personnel regarding state crackdowns and civilian casualties in Balochistan.The leadership transition, confirmed through a statement from group spokesperson Jeeyand Baloch on Nov 14, follows a unanimous vote by the outfit’s senior command council. The move comes just days after the announcement that Bashir Zeb was stepping down as chief.There was also uncertainty surrounding Zeb’s successor after the group said last week that Zeb was transferring all powers to the command council. While pro-Pak military social media accounts circulated rumours of Zeb having been poisoned by a confidante and being killed in Afghanistan, sources described them as false.

Article Title: Redrawing Pakistan: Ministers back 12-province plan but political, constitutional hurdles remain
Article Text:
Pakistan's 12-province proposal gains momentum as senior ministers back restructuring (Representative Image)

What the proposed 12-province map could look like

Political consensus remains the biggest hurdle

What the Constitution requires

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan's proposal to expand its four-province structure to as many as 12 has gathered momentum, with senior ministers backing it in the name of better governance. But the idea faces a major political hurdle: there is no consensus among the country's leading parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh.Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif has argued that Pakistan's growing population requires smaller provinces that can deliver public services more efficiently. Speaking to Geo News, he said the country could consider creating 12 provinces, provided the boundaries were drawn on administrative rather than linguistic, ethnic or political grounds.“If there is a proposal for 12 provinces, then make it 12,” Asif said, adding that new units should not be created to serve “language, ethnicity or political interests”.Pakistan’s interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has also revived the debate, suggesting a referendum to gauge public opinion on the contentious issue. His remarks have fuelled speculation that powerful quarters favour a broader restructuring of Pakistan's administrative map, with reports pointing to a possible constitutional exercise in 2027.No formal roadmap, however, has been announced. The proposed number of provinces, their boundaries and the process for creating them remain undecided.One proposal reported in Pakistani media envisages dividing Punjab into four provinces, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan into three each, and Sindh into two. The plan could involve a nationwide referendum and a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment, although neither has been confirmed as an approved government initiative.Supporters argue that the existing arrangement concentrates too much administrative and financial authority in provincial capitals leaving smaller cities and districts dependent on decisions taken far away.Asif has questioned whether federal funds transferred to provincial governments are reaching local institutions, arguing that decentralisation could bring decision-making and resources closer to communities. Advocates of the proposal say smaller provinces would make public services more accessible and help address uneven development.But the debate is not only about the size of administrative units. It also raises questions about whether creating more provinces would improve governance without stronger local governments and greater financial autonomy for districts.The proposal has exposed differences within the ruling coalition itself. The Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), led by Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, has firmly opposed any division of Sindh, while the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) has yet to settle on a formal position.The two parties are coalition partners in the federal government. The PML-N has said it will announce its position if the matter comes before Parliament, despite some of its leaders backing the creation of smaller provinces.A cabinet member in the Shehbaz Sharif government said reaching agreement would be difficult without the support of the major political parties.The issue has also prompted speculation about a possible understanding between the government and the main opposition, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI). PML-N leader and former federal minister Khawaja Saad Rafique has suggested that the establishment could offer relief to jailed former prime minister Imran Khan in return for PTI's support for the proposed constitutional changes. There has been no confirmation of such a deal.Smaller parties have also entered the debate. The Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) has renewed its demand for new administrative units in Sindh, while Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid chief Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain has called for new provinces to be considered through consultation and in the national interest.The Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party has backed the proposal on administrative grounds, while Jamaat-i-Islami has argued that the creation of new provinces should go hand in hand with strengthening local governments.Even if political parties agree on the broad idea, redrawing provincial boundaries would require a demanding constitutional process.Under Article 239 of Pakistan's Constitution, an amendment requires the support of at least two-thirds of the total membership of both houses of Parliament. If it changes the limits of an existing province, it must also secure the backing of at least two-thirds of the total membership of that province's assembly.That gives provincial parties considerable leverage over any proposed division.A nationwide referendum is not an automatic constitutional requirement for creating provinces. Any such exercise would need its own legal and constitutional basis, and Parliament could not simply be bypassed in deciding the process or framing the questions put to voters.Following a meeting between Pakistan’s president Asif Ali Zardari and prime minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday, a senior government official told news agency PTI that the two leaders had agreed to adhere strictly to the constitutional provisions governing the creation of new provinces. They also agreed that any proposed referendum would require parliamentary approval.Former federal information minister Muhammad Ali Durrani has meanwhile launched a campaign for the restoration of Bahawalpur province and the creation of 11 other smaller administrative units.For now, the proposal remains a subject of political debate rather than an agreed government plan. Any move to redraw the map would require agreement on boundaries, resources, parliamentary representation and the future of provincial institutions — as well as the constitutional numbers to make it happen.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif has argued that Pakistan's growing population requires smaller provinces that can deliver public services more efficiently. But the idea faces a major political hurdle: there is no consensus among the country's leading parties, particularly over the possible division of Sindh.

Article Title: 24 militants, four soldiers killed in separate clashes in Pakistan's Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
(Photo credit: IANS)

At least 24 militants and four Pakistani soldiers, including an army officer, were killed in separate encounters between security forces and militants in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provinces, the Pakistan Army said on Saturday, PTI reported.The army said security forces had carried out multiple intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan since Friday, targeting militant hideouts in the areas of Kolpur, Kardagap and Nushki.During an operation in Kolpur on the intervening night of Friday and Saturday, troops killed eight militants, including a suicide bomber, and recovered a large cache of weapons and ammunition, the military said.The army said the militants used armed quadcopters to target military vehicles on patrol. The attack killed Major Omer Minhas Nasir and Havildar Muhammad Adnan Khan.Separately, security forces conducted operations against militant hideouts in Mir Ali, Datta Khel and surrounding areas of North Waziristan district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.According to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military's media wing, 16 militants were killed in the engagements. Twelve were killed in an operation in Ali Khel, while two each were killed in Mir Ali and Datta Khel.Two soldiers, Havildar Asmat Ali and Naik Aftab Ali, were killed during the operations. The ISPR said both soldiers fought bravely and laid down their lives in the line of duty. It added that the operations had dealt a major blow to the militant network.Weapons and ammunition were recovered from the slain militants, who, according to the military, were involved in several terrorist activities, including the killing of civilians.Pakistan's federal government uses the term 'Fitna al-Khawarij' for militants belonging to the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).
Article Summary: At least 24 militants and four Pakistani soldiers, including an army officer, were killed in separate encounters between security forces and militants. The Pakistan Army said security forces had carried out multiple intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan since Friday, targeting militant hideouts.

Article Title: Pakistani teen mauled to death by tigress released from cage for TikTok video shoot
Article Text:
Pakistani teenager mauled to death after tigress freed for TikTok video in Lahore (Image source: X)

A 19-year-old Pakistani teenager was mauled to death by a tigress after it was let out of its cage for a TikTok video shoot.The victim, identified as Talha, was working at a private breeding facility in Kahna, Lahore district, when the animal attacked him. He was rushed to a private hospital but died while undergoing treatment on Wednesday, according to local reports.Police identified the arrested farm owner as Fayyaz and the TikToker as Noman. Investigators allege that the influencer had visited the property to film a video and asked for the animal to be released from its enclosure. The animal subsequently lost control and attacked the worker, police said.The incident also triggered an investigation into an alleged attempt to conceal the circumstances of the death. Police said efforts were made to portray the attack as an incident involving a dog rather than a big cat. The animal has since been handed over to wildlife authorities.Authorities are examining whether the farm had the necessary permits to keep the animal and whether adequate safety measures were in place at the facility. A case has been registered and investigations into possible negligence are under way.In a statement, Lahore Police said that the pursuit of social media content could not come at the cost of human life. It said all aspects of the alleged negligence and the attempt to conceal the attack would be investigated.There has been some confusion in initial media reports over whether the animal was a tiger or a lion. Lahore Police's statement described it as a tigress.
Article Summary: The victim, identified as Talha, was working at a private breeding facility in Kahna, Lahore district, when the animal attacked him. Investigators allege that the influencer had visited the property to film a video and asked for the animal to be released from its enclosure.

Article Title: Imran Khan-Asim Munir deal? Sisters' release from jail, hospital visit spark buzz in Pakistan
Article Text:
Release of Imran Khan's two sisters and his hospital visit fuel speculation of a possible political understanding with Pakistan's military establishment

PTI ready to make peace?

Nawaz Sharif , Benazir Bhutto precedent

Why a deal may not be straightforward

Is Pakistan witnessing the first signs of a possible thaw between jailed former prime minister Imran Khan and the country's powerful military establishment? The release of two of his sisters and his recent hospital visit for eye treatment have come amid speculation that a political settlement involving Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir has taken place.His sisters, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi were released on Thursday from Lahore's Kot Lakhpat Jail after the Punjab government withdrew their extended detention orders. The two had spent 53 days in custody after being detained ahead of a Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) protest march. Their sister Aleema Khan remains behind bars.The release came a day after Imran Khan was taken from Adiala Jail to Islamabad's Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences for an eye examination and treatment. Doctors administered an injection for an issue affecting his right eye, besides treating his blood pressure. He was discharged in the early hours of Thursday and returned to prison.The developments have coincided with renewed speculation about a possible deal involving Khan and the military establishment. Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi, however, dismissed reports of any behind-the-scenes arrangement on Thursday, saying Khan and his family would receive whatever relief the courts granted them.The possibility of a rapprochement is not entirely new. In August, one of Imran Khan's closest aides, PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari, had told Reuters that the former prime minister would not confront the military if released."If Imran Khan was released tomorrow, hypothetically, he wouldn't do anything that would effectively damage the country," Bukhari had said, describing him as "magnanimous".He had also suggested that Munir could take the initiative to ease tensions, saying the army chief could extend a "healing hand" to the country."That doesn't mean you go loggerheads with the establishment, with the military leader," Bukhari said, adding that personal grievances could be set aside in the national interest.The remarks marked a notable shift in the PTI's public rhetoric after years of confrontation with the military establishment following Khan's ouster in a no-confidence vote in 2022.Bukhari, however, had mentioned that there were no talks between the PTI and the military. He also acknowledged that it was unclear whether Khan himself shared the willingness to reconcile being expressed by party leaders outside prison.The latest speculation has also been fuelled by opposition leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai's claim in October that Khan could be facing pressure to accept an arrangement similar to those involving former prime ministers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto.Sharif left Pakistan in 2000 after being ousted and imprisoned following the military coup led by General Pervez Musharraf. Bhutto spent years abroad in self-imposed exile after her government was dismissed in 1996.Achakzai alleged that the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz and Pakistan Peoples Party were part of a political arrangement that could pave the way for a similar outcome in Khan's case. However, he did not establish that any such agreement had been reached.An exile arrangement could potentially offer a way out of the prolonged confrontation, but there is no confirmation that Khan has agreed to leave Pakistan or that negotiations with Munir are under way.Imran Khan's relationship with the military establishment deteriorated after disagreements over key appointments and foreign policy. He has accused the military leadership, including Munir, of orchestrating his removal. The military denies interfering in politics.Despite being in prison since August 2023, Khan remains the central figure in Pakistan's political confrontation. His party continues to demand his release, access to family members and lawyers, and relief in the cases against him.The PTI's position also raises a crucial question: can its leadership outside prison negotiate or signal a compromise without Khan's explicit approval? Bukhari's August remarks came with the caveat that the former prime minister's own thinking might be different.For now, the signals remain contradictory. Two members of Khan's family have been released, he has received medical treatment, and a senior PTI aide has previously spoken of reconciliation. But the government has denied any political bargain, and there is no evidence of direct negotiations with Munir.Whether the latest developments represent isolated legal and medical decisions or the beginning of a fresh political opening remains the question.
Article Summary: Imran Khan's two sisters were released from jail on Thursday after 53 days in custody. He was also taken to a hospital for an eye examination and treatment. The developments have fuelled speculation about a possible deal involving Khan and the military establishment. Pakistan interior minister dismissed reports of any behind-the-scenes arrangement on Thursday.

Article Title: 'She will have to face music': Bangladesh reaffirms Sheikh Hasina will be arrested if she returns
Article Text:
Former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina has been living in New Delhi since August 5, 2024 (File photo)

As Sheikh Hasina ’s self-announced December deadline to return from India approaches, Dhaka has reaffirmed that the former prime minister will be arrested if she returns to Bangladesh.Shama Obaed, Bangladesh’s state minister for foreign affairs, also called on New Delhi to "honour" its extradition treaty with Dhaka."As soon as she (Hasina) tries to enter Bangladesh, she will be arrested and taken to jail, and the law will take its course," Obaed told Reuters on Sunday."We would like India to honour the extradition treaty and return her as a convict. The law will take its course. She will have to face the music," the minister added.Sheikh Hasina, the daughter of Bangladesh's founding father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, has been living in New Delhi since August 5, 2024, when she resigned and fled the country following a student-led uprising that brought down her Awami League government. The United Nations estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.The former PM was tried in absentia and convicted of crimes against humanity linked to the July Uprising, as the movement is known in Bangladesh. She has dismissed the verdict as an act of political vendetta.In August, Sheikh Hasina announced plans to return to Bangladesh by December. She has since applied for a new passport and identity card, but the Bangladesh Nationalist Party-led government has turned down both requests.The standoff has prompted Awami League supporters to take to the streets. The party, which was banned by the interim administration of Muhammad Yunus, announced nationwide protests and rallies this month in support of its leader.Over the past 10 days, police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and arson attacks targeting vehicles across at least 28 districts, leaving several police officers and civilians injured, local media reported.Obaed described the violence as a survival tactic by Sheikh Hasina's "politically bankrupt political party."The foreign affairs minister also responded to a report that India had set conditions for extraditing Sheikh Hasina."There have been no official discussions with India about sending an aircraft to bring Hasina back. … We want balanced ties that do not compromise Bangladesh's 'dignity, self-respect and interests'," she added.New Delhi has repeatedly maintained that Dhaka's request for Sheikh Hasina's extradition remains under consideration.
Article Summary: Sheikh Hasina has been living in New Delhi since August 5, 2024. She resigned and fled the country following a student-led uprising that brought down her Awami League government. The former PM was tried in absentia and convicted of crimes against humanity.
